en: The Mālinīvijayottara Tantra, First Chapter: On Emanation (Sṛṣṭyadhikāra).
1.1ab: Victorious are those [teachings] capable of destroying the adversaries of the bliss of the world.
1.1cd: The rays of the moon of knowledge emerging from the mouth of the Supreme Lord; 1.2ab:
The savior of those submerged in the ocean of the world, [leading them] to the end of rebirth;
1.2cd: Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sanātana, and Sanandana.
1.3ab: The great sages Nārada, Agastya, Saṃvarta, Vasiṣṭha, and others, 1.3cd:
desiring to know the supreme reality and directed toward Śiva and Śakti, 1.4ab:
having worshipped him according to the prescribed rite, spoke to him with great joy.
1.4cd: "We have come desiring the attainment of the yoga of the Blessed One.
1.5ab: "And since that [attainment] cannot occur without yoga, therefore, please teach it.
1.5cd: Thus was he addressed by those sages who desired yoga.
1.6ab: Having bowed to Maheśvara, he, with a joyful soul, replied:
1.6cd: "Listen, I shall fully proclaim [this teaching] which bestows the fruit of all accomplishments (siddhi). 1.7ab: It is the Mālinīvijaya Tantra, issued from the mouth of the Supreme Lord."
1.7cd: To Umā’s Lord, the bestower of enjoyment and liberation, who is worshipped by the immortals;
1.8ab: Goddess Umā, having prostrated before him as he stood in his own place, spoke this:
1.8cd: "The *Siddhayogeśvarītantra*, which extends to ninety million verses."
1.9ab: That which was previously spoken by you, spread across three divisions, 1.9cd: in the *Mālinīvijaya Tantra* characterized by thirty million verses;
1.10ab: the path of yoga has been proclaimed by you in great detail, O Maheśvara.
1.10cd: Furthermore, its summary has been proclaimed in twelve [thousand verses]. 1.11ab:
That too, being extensive, cannot be grasped by those of small intellect. 1.11cd: Therefore, having condensed it for the benefit of those of limited intelligence, [it is presented] in brief.
1.12ab: O Supreme Lord, out of your grace, tell me that which brings about all accomplishments.
1.12cd: Thus addressed by the Goddess, the Sovereign of the Universe then spoke, smiling.
1.13ab: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the Siddhayogeśvarīmata.
1.13cd: That which has not been told to anyone is the *Mālinīvijayottara*. 1.14ab: This too was formerly obtained by me from Aghora, the Supreme Self.
1.14cd: That which is to be accepted and that which is to be abandoned must be understood according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
1.15ab: Śiva, Śakti, the Vidyās, the Īśas, the Mantras, the Mantreśvaras, and the Aṇus;
1.15cd: these six are declared to be that which is to be accepted by those who seek the fruit.
1.16ab: Impurity (mala), action (karma), Māyā, and the entire world belonging to Māyā.

1.16cd: It is declared that everything is to be abandoned; this is the determined reality to be known. 1.17ab: Having known this and having relinquished it, one shall obtain the fruit of all accomplishments. 1.17cd: Therein resides the Lord, the doer of all, the peaceful, the omniscient, the maker of all, the sovereign.
1.18ab: He is both with parts and without parts, infinite; His power is likewise of that same nature.

1.18cd: Desiring to create the world, at the very beginning of creation, by His own will, 1.19ab: He awakened eight individual souls (*pudgala*) who were [previously] isolated in pure consciousness (*vijñānakevala*).
1.19cd: Aghora, Paramaghora, Ghorarūpa, and Tadānana; 1.20ab: Bhīma, Bhīṣaṇa, Vamana, and likewise Pivana—these eight perform the functions of maintenance, destruction, protection, and grace.
1.21ab: Having then again joined the mantra and the lord of the mantra in purity, 1.21cd:
he likewise created seventy million mantras together with their maṇḍalas.
1.22ab: All these great-souled mantras bestow all fruits.
1.22cd: The Self is to be known as fourfold; therein, the *vijñānakevala* (the solitary one consisting of consciousness) [is the first].

1.23ab: That which is joined with *mala* alone is the *pralayakevala* (the solitary one in dissolution), and that which is joined with its *karman* (action). 1.23cd: They maintain that *mala* is ignorance (*ajñāna*), the cause of the sprout of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).
1.24ab: Action, consisting of merit and demerit, is characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth.

1.24cd: By the power of the Lord’s will, the desire for enjoyment arises in this [individual soul]. 1.25ab: For the sake of accomplishing the means of enjoyment, the King of Mantras [arises] for this one who desires enjoyment.
1.25cd: Having entered into Māyā with his powers, he brought forth the world.
1.26ab: And she is one, all-pervading, subtle, partless, and the storehouse of the universe.
1.26cd: She is said to be without beginning or end, the sovereign mistress of the inauspicious, and free from decay.
1.27ab: She gave birth to the principle of *kalā*, through union with which the Person came into being.
1.27cd: Once he had acquired the capacity for agency, he then brought forth *vidyā* and *rāga*.
1.28ab: *Vidyā* discriminates for him between action and its causes and effects.
1.28cd: Passion colors him even toward his own impure enjoyments;
1.29ab: Necessity yokes this individual (pudgala) to his own karma; 1.29cd: Time also measures him, abiding in its divisions such as *tuṭi* and the rest.

1.30ab: From that very *kalā*-tattva, he then created the Unmanifest (*avyakta*); 1.30cd: from that [the Unmanifest], the eight qualities (*guṇa*); from those, the intellect (*dhī*); and from the intellect, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkṛti*). 1.31ab: That [ego-sense] is threefold; from the *taijasa* [type of ego-sense], the mind (*manas*), which is the lord of the senses, was born.
1.31cd: From the *vaikārika* [ahaṃkāra] arise the sense organs; from the third [the *bhūtādi*] arise the subtle elements (*tanmātras*).
1.32ab: The ear, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose are the organs of cognition (*buddhīndriyas*).
1.32cd: The organs of action (*karmendriyas*) are, in order: speech, hands, anus, genitals, and feet.

1.33ab: This sphere of transmigratory existence extends from the category of *kalā* down to the earth. 1.33cd: By its will, it causes the entire world, beginning with the oceans, to revolve. 1.34ab: The supreme differentiation of the categories, beginning with *kalā*, which exists as the [constituent] worlds (*bhuvana*).
1.34cd: He himself created him for the sake of the enjoyment and the attainment of enjoyment by the *bhogins*.

1.35ab: Thus, those who are endowed with [the principles] beginning with *kalā* and ending with *dharā* (earth) are to be known as *sakalas* (conditioned souls). 1.35cd: This is to be understood by those who desire to destroy that state [of bondage].
1.36ab: Even in these three states, being completely pervaded by the power of Śiva, which has the nature of concealment, [beings] perform their various activities. 1.37ab:
Thus, throughout the entire world, by virtue of the specific capacity of the Rudras—
1.37cd: [He bestowed] one hundred and eighteen [mantras], beginning with the *aṅguṣṭhamātra*.
1.38ab: Having personally favored them, Śiva appointed them to the status of Lords of Mantras (*mantreśvara*).
1.38cd: Having attained their own respective spheres, they [serve] those who seek the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.

1.39ab: They bestow upon Brahmā and the others a fruit equal to their own power; 1.39cd: they [bestow it] upon the sages, and those great lords [bestow it] in turn upon the Manvantaras. 1.40ab: They proclaim the knowledge of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted as taught by Śiva.
1.40cd: As soon as the world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, had come into being, 1.41ab:
three and a half crores of mantras were appointed by Śiva; 1.41cd: having bestowed grace upon the multitude of individual souls (aṇu), they proceeded to the state free from affliction.

1.42ab: Thus, at a certain time, by virtue of his own fitness, this self becomes connected with the peaceful power of Śiva, which bestows the fruit of liberation. 1.42cd–43ab: Through that connection, someone is liberated from that very moment.
1.43cd: The identity with ignorance is removed for someone;
1.44ab: Possessed by the power of Rudra, desiring to go forth by the will of Śiva, 1.44cd: he is led toward a true guru for the sake of attaining enjoyment and liberation.

1.45ab: Having propitiated him and then received the Śaṅkara-initiation from the gratified [deity], 1.45cd: one shall go to Śiva at the fall of the body, either immediately or through [gradual] enjoyment. 1.46ab: Having obtained the initiation into Yoga and having understood Yoga, one should practice it thoroughly.
1.46cd: He attains the perfection of yoga, and at its conclusion, the eternal state.
1.47ab: Having reached the supreme state by means of this sequential yoga, 1.47cd: he does not return to the condition of a bound animal (paśu), but abides in his own pure self.

1.48ab: For this self is indeed fourfold, and again it is fourfold; 1.48cd: the pure self is recited according to the distinctions of being a teacher and so forth. 1.49ab: The Guru and the Sādhaka alike should perform the triad beginning with the "eternal" (nitya).
1.49cd: By the command of Śiva, one must always follow both [the path] and the other for as long as one lives.
1.50ab: That which is to be adopted and that which is to be abandoned—this has been fully proclaimed.
1.50cd: Having known this, the entirety of what is to be known, one shall become a secret treasury of all accomplishments.

Thus ends the first chapter, the Chapter on Pervasion (*vyāptyadhikāra*), in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*. 2.1ab: Now, [we shall describe] these very principles (*tattva*), beginning with Earth (*dharā*) and so forth, in their proper sequence.
2.1cd: The manifold expansion (prapañca) is described briefly for the sake of the yogis’ accomplishment of yoga.
2.2ab: The principle of earth (dharātattva) is differentiated by means of the distinction between the possessor of power and the power itself.
2.2cd: Together with its own essential nature, it should be known as fifteenfold.
2.3ab: Those beginning with Śiva and ending with Sakalātman are proclaimed to be the possessors of power (śaktimant).
2.3cd: Their powers (śaktis) should likewise be understood by the wise in exactly the same way.
2.4ab: Thus, this great multitude of principles (tattvas), from water up to the Root-nature (mūla), [has been described].

2.4cd: That [reality] should be known as divided by these distinct categories by those who desire its fruit. 2.5ab: By this very same method, from the *puruṣa-tattva* down to *kalā*, 2.5cd: the *pralayākala* is to be known as thirteenfold, like Rudra.
2.6ab: In the same way, Māyā is to be known as ninefold; the Jñānakevalas [are ninefold].
2.6cd: Likewise, the Mantras are sevenfold, and the Mantranāyakas are fivefold.
2.7ab: The Mantreśvaras and Īśānas are threefold; Śiva himself is not divided.
2.7cd: This infinite division has been briefly described; in its full detail, it is as follows.
2.8ab: In this way, the garland of worlds (bhuvanamālā) is also clearly divided by these same divisions.
2.8cd: It should be understood by yogins for the sake of attaining yoga-perfection, being honored through yoga.

2.9ab: O Daughter of Śaṅkara, whoever knows even one of these principles (*tattva*) and worlds (*bhuvana*), 2.9cd: he too shall obtain the fruit of yoga. 2.10ab: But he who knows all these principles exactly as they are—
2.10cd: That guru is declared to be equal to me, for he reveals the potency of the mantra.
2.11ab: Men who have been seen, spoken to, or touched by him with a joyful heart, 2.11cd:
are liberated from sins, even those committed over seven lifetimes.
2.12ab: Furthermore, those living beings who have been initiated by him and impelled by Śiva, 2.12cd: having attained the fruit according to their desire, go to the supreme state.
2.13ab: Therein, the immersion into the power of Rudra is eternally established.
2.13cd: And when that [state] exists, one should observe these signs belonging to it.
2.14ab: Among them, this is the first sign: unwavering devotion to Rudra. 2.14cd: The second would be the accomplishment of mantra, which produces immediate conviction.
2.15ab: And mastery over all sentient beings is remembered as the third characteristic;
2.15cd: the accomplishment of undertakings already begun they call the fourth sign.
2.16ab: The fifth is declared to be poetic composition, charming and adorned with figures of speech.
2.16cd: And the knowledge of the meaning of all scriptures arises in him spontaneously.
2.17ab: The immersion into the power of Rudra (rudraśakti-samāveśa) is taught as fivefold.
2.17cd: O fair-faced one, it is distinguished by the divisions of the elements (bhūta), the principles (tattva), the self (ātman), the lords of mantras (mantreśa), and the powers (śakti).
2.18ab: That which is designated as the "elements" (bhūta) is fivefold, while the next is thirtyfold.

2.18cd: That called the "self" (ātman) is said to be threefold, and that designated as "mantra" is tenfold. 2.19ab: Furthermore, that designated as "power" (śakti) should be known from the perspective of ultimate reality to be twofold.

2.19cd: This immersion (samāveśa) is proclaimed to be divided into fifty varieties. 2.20ab: This is declared to be the individual (āṇava); the empowered (śākta) is likewise remembered as being of this same kind.
2.20cd: In this way, one should discern that even the divine (śāmbhava) is divided by these same distinctions.
2.21ab: Through the visualization of the utterance, the organs of action, meditation, the phonemes, and the locations;
2.21cd: whatever immersion (*samāveśa*) may arise is correctly called *āṇava* [empowerment].
2.22ab: Contemplating the reality devoid of utterance by means of the mind alone...

2.22cd: That state of immersion which one attains is here called *śākta*. 2.23ab: That immersion which arises for one who thinks of nothing at all, through being awakened by the Guru, 2.23cd: is declared to be *śāmbhava*.
2.24ab: These one hundred and fifty varieties have been declared in their proper sequence;
2.24cd: whether in brief or in detail, there is no end to their enumeration.
2.25ab: Wise men should not conceive of any difference in the fruit of consciousness here.
2.25cd: Another division shall also be stated in brief; let it be understood.

2.26ab: The sequence of all entries (*āveśa*) is divided by the wise into five types according to the distinctions of waking, dreaming, and so forth. 2.26cd: It should be thoroughly known as distinct from its own respective functions.
2.27ab: In that regard, the triad consisting of essential nature (*svarūpa*), power (*śakti*), and the manifest (*sakala*)— 2.27cd: this is the waking state within the fifteenfold division.
2.28ab: Two [states], the unmanifest (*akala*), are to be correctly understood as belonging to the dreaming and deep sleep states.
2.28cd: The group consisting of the Mantras and so forth, up to Tatpuruṣa and Īśāna, is known as the Fourth (turya).
2.29ab: O fair-faced one, Śakti and Śambhu are to be understood as being in the state Beyond the Fourth (turyātīta).
2.29cd: In the division consisting of thirteen, both are of the nature of the Akala [state].
2.30ab: The Mantras, Mantreśvaras, and Mantreśānas, as well as Śakti and Śambhu, are proclaimed [to exist];
2.30cd: even in the division of the Pralayākala, both [Mantra and Mantreśvara] exist in the Vijñānakala.
2.31ab: The Mantras, Mantreśvaras, and Mantreśānas, as well as Śakti and Īśa, are likewise present as before.
2.31cd: When the ninefold division has been proclaimed, [there are] one's own mantras and the lords of mantras;
2.32ab: Their lords, the Śaktis, and Śambhus—these five states are proclaimed.
2.32cd: As before, even in the sevenfold division, there are one's own [mantras], the lords of mantras, the lords, and the Śaktis.
2.33ab: O lady of excellent complexion, these five alone are to be fully known as Śiva: 2.33cd: Sva, Śakti, Sanijeśāna, Śakti, and Śambhu constitute the pentad.
2.34ab: In the triad, one should discern the states of Sva, Śakti, Śaktīcchā, and Śiva.
2.34cd: Because it exercises sovereignty over its own functions and because it impels those [functions] dependent upon it;
2.35ab: Because desire ceases and it remains in its own state, although undivided, it is fivefold.
2.35cd: Thus, the reality is proclaimed as that which should be known within this fivefold division.
2.36ab: Furthermore, the distinction between the designations of these states is now revealed.
2.36cd: *Piṇḍastha* and *Sarvatobhadra* are considered to be the two names for the waking state (*jāgrat*).
2.37ab: They maintain that *padastha* and *vyāpti* likewise possess two names each, [the latter] being the dreaming state (*svapna*).
2.37cd: But the state established in form is the Great Pervasion; even for one in deep sleep, that [state] is twofold.
2.38ab: Accumulation and the state beyond form are correctly declared to be the Fourth (turya). 2.38cd: The wise maintain that the state beyond the Fourth (turyātīta) is the Great Accumulation.
2.39ab: This distinction has been proclaimed according to the separate divisions of the principles (tattva).

2.39cd: All principles are indeed these five; listen now as they are [explained]. 2.40ab: That portion which is intended as the object of presiding over among those designated as the principles of the elements (bhūtatattva) is [the gross element].
2.40cd: They call that "residing in the body" (piṇḍastha); they know the other as "residing in the word" (padastha).
2.41ab: The mantras, their lords, and the Lord (Īśa) together are proclaimed as "residing in form" (rūpastha).
2.41cd: The Supreme Power (parā śakti), though engaged in activity, is beyond form (rūpātīta) and free from affliction.
2.42ab: Free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), free from appearance (*nirābhāsa*), pure, and established in its own self;
2.42cd: Śiva is to be known as transcending all, by knowing whom one is liberated.
2.43ab: But the fourfold [state] is that which resides in the body (*piṇḍastha*), the unawakened, and the awakened.
2.43cd: It is fourfold: awakened (*prabuddha*), well-awakened (*suprabuddha*), and established in the state (*padastha*).
2.44ab: Moving and returning (*gatāgata*), well-dispersed (*suvikṣipta*), conjoined (*saṅgata*), and well-composed (*susamāhita*).
2.44cd: Those who contemplate yoga should know that it is established in form (*rūpasaṃstha*) in these four ways.

2.45ab: It is declared to be vast, tranquil, and exceedingly serene; furthermore, it is beyond the mind, infinite, the goal of all, and eternally manifest. 2.46ab: In that accumulation, this is to be known as the one that abides within the Great.
2.46cd: Thus, the path has been described in five ways; now it is explained in three ways.

2.47ab: That which extends up to the Vijñānākala is declared to be the *ātmatattva* (the principle of the self). 2.47cd: That which ends with Īśvara is called *vidyā*; they know the remainder to be the state of Śiva (*śivapada*).
2.48ab: Thus, the path (adhvan) has been described there as divided by these distinctions. 2.48cd: Now, the simultaneous differentiation of all the paths is being proclaimed.
2.49ab: [These are] the earthly (pārthiva), the primal (prākṛta), the illusory (māyīya), and the empowered (śākta).
2.49cd: Thus, this fourfold egg has been described in brief.
2.50ab: Two of them are separate and innumerable; each one [of the other two] is distinct.
2.50cd: The first is pervaded by the Dhārikā [power], and therein a single principle (tattva) is recognized.
2.51ab: One should meditate upon each individual syllable of the *kṣa* [mantra], corresponding to the syllables of the words, within the worlds.
2.51cd: From the world of Kālāgni up to the supreme city of Vīrabhadra;
2.52ab: This should be known as the sixteen cities; thus the sixfold path (*ṣaḍadhvan*) is proclaimed.
2.52cd: And the second [wheel] is the Āpyāyinī; therein one should observe the principles (tattvas).
2.53ab: These are the twenty-three beginning with earth (pṛthivī), as well as the letters beginning with *dh*.
2.53cd: There are five words, six mantras, and fifty-six cities.
2.54ab: By means of Bodhinī, there are seven principles (tattvas) and four cities;
2.54cd: In the third [cakra], there are seven phonemes (varṇas), and two pairs of padas and mantras. 2.55ab: But by means of Utpūyinī, they know that in the fourth [cakra] there are three principles.
2.55cd: One should perceive the three castes as one mantra and one word.
2.56ab: In brief, one should know there to be eighteen worlds.
2.56cd: The supreme Śiva-tattva is peaceful; therein, the *kalā* [called] Avakāśadā provides space.
2.57ab: One should discern the sixteen vowels as the mantra and the single word.
2.57cd: Thus, the sixfold path has been briefly proclaimed.
2.58ab: Since the entire universe, both pure and impure, originates from the Egg of Brahmā (brahmāṇḍa).
2.58cd: Therefore, everything is held to be pure by these pure cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas).
2.59ab: O lady of good vows, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara— 2.59cd: among these, the four Lords (patayaḥ) should be understood as distinct from one another, yet [ultimately] peaceful.
2.60ab: For whoever is superior in qualities compared to another is said to be above that one.
2.60cd: All this has been told to you; what else do you wish to ask?
Thus ends the second chapter, the Section on Pervasion (*vyāptyadhikāra*), in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*.
The third chapter: On the Extraction of Mantras.

3.1ab: Thus addressed by the one who brings joy to the world, the Great Goddess, having prostrated, spoke these words again to the Lord of the World: 3.1cd: [She spoke] this speech once more to the Lord of the World after bowing down.
3.2ab: Thus it is, O Mahādeva; it has been declared otherwise than this. 3.2cd: Just as it was told, so it is known from the beginning in its proper sequence.
3.3ab: [O] Supreme Lord, [the names] which denote the forms of the entities beginning with Śiva...
3.3cd: "Now I wish to hear [this]; by your grace, you ought to speak.
3.4ab: Thus addressed by the Great Goddess, Hara, the remover of the world's suffering, 3.4cd: spoke the mantras that are to be recited, which have come down through the lineage of tradition.
3.5ab: That power which is said to be inherent in the Creator of the universe, 3.5cd: O Goddess, that very power becomes His will when He desires to emit [the world].
3.6ab: Listen now to how, although it is one, it attains multiplicity.
3.6cd: It should be known with firm certainty that "it is thus" and not otherwise.
3.7ab: That which makes this known in this world is called the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).
3.7cd: But when [one intends], "May this object become such as it is," then...
3.8ab: That which, being born at that very moment, performs such and such [actions] is here called "action" (*kriyā*).
3.8cd: Thus, although this [action] possesses two forms, it further attains infinity through its divisions.
3.9ab: By the power of the limiting adjuncts of objects, she, the Sovereign Lady, becomes manifold like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*).
3.9cd: Therein, first of all, having entered into meditative absorption, she differentiates her maternal nature.
3.10ab: Mālinī is divided twofold, ninefold, and indeed fiftyfold.
3.10cd: Due to the division consisting of seed-syllables (*bīja*) and womb-syllables (*yoni*), it is twofold; the vowels are considered to be the seeds.
3.11ab: And the Yoni is remembered as ninefold by means of the letters beginning with *ka*, according to the division of the classes (*varga*).
3.11cd: Distinct through the differentiation of its phonemes, it blazes with fifty rays.
3.12ab: Here, Śiva is called the Seed (*bīja*) and Śakti is called the Yoni.
3.12cd: And every power of Śambhu is praised as being expressive. 3.13ab: Here, the group of eight beginning with Aghora is to be known in their proper sequence.
3.13cd: That very same [group], through the differentiation of its powers, is the group of eight beginning with Māheśvarī.
3.14ab: Māheśī, Brāhmaṇī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī;
3.14cd: Aindrī, Yāmyā, Cāmuṇḍā, and Yogīśī—these are considered [the eight].
3.15ab: O fair-faced one, they are divided into five hundred varieties, numbering that many.
3.15cd: They were fashioned by the Supreme Lord as the designators of the Rudras;
3.16ab: and in the same manner, [he fashioned] the Śaktis, equal in number to them, in their proper sequence. 3.16cd: I shall explain everything regarding their divisions; listen accordingly.
3.17ab: Amṛta, Amṛtapūrṇa, Amṛtābha, and Amṛtadrava; 3.17cd: Amṛtaugha, Amṛtormi, and another, Amṛtasyandana;
3.18ab: Amṛtāṅga, Amṛtavapuḥ, and indeed Amṛtodgāra.
3.18cd: Amṛtāsya, Amṛtatanu, and likewise Amṛtasecana;
3.19ab: Tanmūrti, Amṛteśa, and another, Sarvāmṛtadhara;
3.19cd: These sixteen are proclaimed as those born from the seed-syllable of Rudra.
3.20ab: Jaya, Vijaya, Jayanta, and Aparājita;
3.20cd: Sujaya, Jayarudra, Jayakīrti, and Jayāvaha;
3.21ab: Jayamūrti, Jayotsāha, Jayada, and Jayavardhana.
3.21cd: Bala, Atibala, Balabhadra, and Balaprada;
3.22ab: Balāvaha, Balavān, Baladātā, and Baleśvara;
3.22cd: Nandana, Sarvatobhadra, Bhadramūrti, and Śivaprada.
3.23ab: Sumanas, Spṛhaṇa, Durga, Bhadrakāla, Manonuga;
3.23cd: Kauśika, Kālaviśveśa, Suśiva, Kopavardhana. 3.24ab: These thirty-four, born from the womb, have been proclaimed.
3.24cd: These very powers, having come under the influence of the female recitation, [are present] here.
3.25ab: Arising from seed and womb, they rest upon the power of Rudra.
3.25cd: Because the denoters are infinite, no exhaustive enumeration exists.
3.26ab: With this [scripture], which contains within it the meaning of all treatises, 3.26cd:
the Supreme Lord, by his own will, awakened Aghora. 3.27ab:
Having been fully awakened by that [scripture], he agitated the womb with his powers.
3.27cd: The Lord created letters with sounds identical to those [mantras], in the same number.
3.28ab: When embraced by those [letters], they bestow the fruit of all desires upon the foremost of practitioners. 3.28cd: This is so, O Goddess worshipped by heroes; it is not otherwise.
3.29ab: By them this entire universe, including gods, asuras, and humans, is pervaded;
3.29cd: from them the scriptures and the Vedas arise again and again.
3.30ab: Of the infinite and manifold Śiva-śakti, the Great Soul...
3.30cd: O Great Goddess, due to the difference in their effects, they are declared to be threefold.
3.31ab: They cause the individual souls (aṇu) who are completely immersed in sense objects to fall lower and lower.
3.31cd: Those others which embrace the Rudra-souls are known as the most terrible (ghoratara).
3.32ab: Those [powers] which, as before, produce attachment to the fruits of mixed karma;
3.32cd: and which obstruct the path to liberation, they are the terrible *parāpara* powers.
3.33ab: As before, they bestow upon the multitude of living beings the fruit that is the abode of Śiva.
3.33cd: Those who know [the truth] have declared that the supreme powers of Śiva are non-terrible (aghorāḥ).

3.34ab: Just as these remain as the ultimate ground even for the entire aggregate of individual souls (aṇu), 3.34cd: so has it been told to you: the power of Śambhu is one alone, the power of Śaṅkara.

3.35ab: Another distinction of this [vidyā] is now explained according to the difference in its expressive words (vācaka), 3.35cd: for the sake of the successful attainment of desired fruits by those who follow the mantras and tantras.
3.36ab: In the case of ritual applications of placement (nyāsa) that lack specific injunctions, the knower of mantras [should proceed as follows].
3.36cd: One should deposit the Mālinī [mantra] of distinct origin for the sake of the body of Śakti.
3.37ab: *Śikhā* (the crest) is Ṛ Ṝ Ḷ Ḹ; *śiromālā* (the garland of the head) is Tha; *mastaka* (the head) is [Ma].
3.37cd: The eyes are Ca Dha; the nose is Vai; the ocean is Ī; the ears are Ṇu Ṇū.
3.38ab: The *baka* group [of letters] is located in the mouth, teeth, tongue, and speech.
3.38cd: *Va*, *bha*, and *ya* are in the throat, the right shoulder and so forth, and the shoulders; *ḍa* and *ḍha* are in the two arms.
3.39ab: *Ṭha* is in the two hands; *jha* and *ña* are in the fingers (*śākhā*); *ja*, *ra*, and *ṭa* are in the trident and the skull-bowl (*kapālaka*).

3.39cd: *pa* is the heart; *cha* and *la* are the breasts; *ā* with *sa* and the visarga (*ḥ*) is the milk. 3.40ab: That which follows is said to be the life-force (*prāṇa*); *ṣa* and *kṣa* are located in the belly and the navel.
3.40cd: *ma*, *śa*, and *ta* go to the hips, the private parts, and the pair of thighs; likewise, the knees.
3.41ab: Likewise, the letters *e* and *ai* are the two shanks; the letters *da* and *pha* following them are the two feet.
3.41cd: From these, the sciences and the mantras are to be extracted; listen as to how. 3.42ab: One should then form the speech [the letter *va*] together with the bindu from the right shank.
3.42cd: Then, the fourth tooth is joined with that same shank. 3.43ab: The staff is joined with the right knee; the breath (prāṇa) is joined to the staff. 3.43cd:
Separately, the two teeth-staffs located on the heart, the staff, and the hips are as before.
3.44ab: Then, as before, one should take the letter *u* joined with the *bindu*, followed by the letter *da*.

3.44cd: Having extracted the staff (*daṇḍa*) alone, it is again conjoined with the left-hand mudrā. 3.45ab: It is joined with the right knee, and the heart is conjoined with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) together with the individual soul (*jīvātman*).
3.45cd: Having placed the tooth as before, and likewise the staff alone; 3.46ab:
The buttock with the right thumb, and the second [tooth] with the tongue and the twice-born [index finger]; 3.46cd:
Together with the nose and the right peak, and then the buttock alone.
3.47ab: Again, in the same manner, one should place the crown of the head, then the belly alone;
3.47cd: then the ear joined with the right knee, and the throat alone;
3.48ab: having placed the hip alone, [one should place] the heart joined with the tongue.
3.48cd: Having raised the face alone with the first knee and the vital breath;
3.49ab: And the fourfold staff of the trident—therein, the first two are upright;
3.49cd: At its end, one should place the left foot and a fallen skull.
3.50ab: Thereafter, from the end of Paramaghora up to Pādyaka and so forth, it is as before.
3.50cd: She is declared to be Parāparā, and Aparā is now described. 3.51ab: First, one should install [the mantra] ending with Aghora, and then again the vital breath (prāṇa) joined with the bindu.
3.51cd: Having performed the placement [of the mantra] accompanied by the *vāmamudrā*, one offers the water for the feet (*pādya*) with the *kādi* [mantra] as before.
3.52ab: This other [method] has been fully explained; now hear of the supreme power (*śakti*) of Rudra.
3.52cd: By the mere utterance of which, the mantras attain a state of being face-to-face [with the deity].

3.53ab: The slender body trembles and there is a sudden leaping up; 3.53cd: [The practitioner may perform] the binding of mudrās, singing, and even the howling of a jackal; 3.54ab: Or he may engage in the narration and so forth of matters past and future.
3.54cd: The life-force (jīva), accompanied by the left shank, has come down through the lineage of succession.
3.55ab: By this [practice], this supreme accomplishment is attained, which bestows the fruit of all desires.
3.55cd: This should never be given to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who lacks devotion.
3.56ab: Rudra, the power of Rudra (rudra-śakti), and the Guru—these three are equal.
3.56cd: To him who beholds them with devotion, O fair-faced one, [the initiation] should be given. 3.57ab: It should also be received by the disciple when the Guru has been fully satisfied.
3.57cd: By means of [knowledge of] the body, substances, consciousness, purification, ritual action, qualities, and so forth;
3.58ab: When she has been awakened by that teacher with a joyful heart, 3.58cd: then she should be known as the bestower of accomplishment, and not otherwise, O Goddess worshipped by heroes.
3.59ab: The eight yoginīs of great power are produced from the higher and lower limbs.
3.59cd: They consist, respectively, of five, six, five, four, two, three, and two syllables.
3.60ab: They should be known as having seven and eleven syllables, accompanied by one and a half syllables each.
3.60cd: The *jīva* [syllable] consists of six long vowels, each distinguished by its respective class [of consonants].

3.61ab: The limbs (*gātra*) of the triple knowledge (*vidyātraya*) are formed by the short vowels, and the faces (*vaktra*) by five [long vowels]. 3.61cd: With five *oṃ* syllables, the mantra becomes the heart (*hṛdaya*) of the limbs of the *vidyā*.
3.62ab: Oṃ amṛte tejomālini svāhā—this [mantra] is adorned with eleven words. 3.62cd: This is declared to be the Brahmaśiras, O Dear One. 3.63ab:
"Vedavedini hūṃ phaṭ," preceded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ).

3.63cd: Rudrāṇī, consisting of eight syllables, is to be known as the *śikhā* [mantra] for the group of vidyās. 3.64ab: Beginning with the *praṇava* and ending with *svāhā*, "to Vajrin, to Vajradhara," 3.64cd: this eleven-syllable mantra is remembered as the *varma* [armour], highly praised by Puruṣṭuta.

3.65ab: Ślīpada, Paśuśabda, and Hūṃphaḍanta beginning with Bhava— 3.65cd: this is declared as the supreme Pāśupata mantra, consisting of six and a half syllables. 3.66ab: With the long vowels *la*, *ra*, *ṭa*, *kṣa*, *va*, and *ya*, joined with *sūma* and provided with the bindu (*m*).
3.66cd: The wise one should visualize Indra and the others with the short vowels, and their weapons likewise.

3.67ab: Similarly, Viṣṇu and Prajāpati are to be visualized from the [nasal] *nāsā* and the vowel *au*. 3.67cd: The first and third *svara*s (a and i), however, are the designators of the lotus and the discus.
3.68ab: Thus the collection of mantras has been proclaimed, which bestows the fruit of all desires.
3.68cd: For the sake of the yogis’ accomplishment of yoga—what else do you wish to ask?
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Extraction of Mantras," in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*.
The Fourth Chapter: On the Characteristics of Yoga.
4.1ab: Then, having heard this, the sages, their eyes filled with joy, 4.1cd: bowed to the slayer of Krauñca and spoke these words once more.

4.2ab: When questioned by the Goddess regarding the procedure for the path of yoga, the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), who had made that very promise, spoke. 4.2cd: For what purpose was the definition of mantra stated?
4.3ab: Thus addressed by them, the highly intelligent Kārttikeya [replied].
4.3cd: He spoke these words to dispel their doubt:
4.4ab: They maintain that yoga is the oneness of an object with another object, 4.4cd:
namely that which is called "the object of knowledge" (*jñeya*), for the sake of establishing its status as something to be abandoned and so forth.
4.5ab: Even that knowledge, though it possesses two forms, cannot be known without [the other].
4.5cd: For the sake of its establishment, the knowledge which has been described was spoken by Śiva.
4.6ab: Furthermore, the characteristics of mantra are sufficient for the complete accomplishment of yoga with seed (*sabījayoga*).
4.6cd: And there is no eligibility for the Yoga of Śiva without initiation (dīkṣā).
4.7ab: That [initiation] is declared to be twofold, through the distinction between ritual action (kriyā) and knowledge (jñāna).
4.7cd: It must be performed in these two ways; therefore, this has been illustrated.
4.8ab: Nor would eligibility for yoga alone arise through this [initiation];
4.8cd: rather, eligibility for mantra and liberation also [arise] through Śiva-initiation. 4.9ab: Having heard these words of her Lord, her body was covered in horripilation.
4.9cd: Furthermore, O best of sages, my mother spoke these words again: 4.10ab:
Within the body of Abhinnamālinī, the principles (tattvas), the worlds (bhuvanas), 4.10cd:
the kalās, the words (padas), and the mantras have been correctly comprehended.
4.11ab: But as for that Mālinī of mine, O God, which you described as having a divided source (bhinnayoni), 4.11cd: tell me how these [mantras] are situated within its limbs.
4.12ab: Thus addressed by the Great Goddess, Bhairava, the bestower of abundant enjoyments, [replied:]
4.12cd: Illuminating the quarters of space with the radiance of shimmering moonbeams;
4.13ab: Whose command is cherished by the garlands upon the crests of the gods and asuras;
4.13cd: Spoke these sweet words, which were intended to cause no distress.
4.14ab: O Goddess, that Mālinī of diverse origins which has been described by me, 4.14cd: I shall now fully explain all of that according to its actual state within its constituent parts.
4.15ab: The phoneme *pha* is designated as the earth-element (*dharātattva*), followed in sequence by the letters beginning with *da* and ending with *jha*.
4.15cd: One should recognize [the signs] beginning with the twenty-third up to the *pradhāna*.
4.16ab: And in the first group of seven, there are seven [signs] beginning with the *puruṣa*, as before.
4.16cd: Among the *iṅghas*, one should know three; from knowledge, up to the end of the *sakala*.
4.17ab: In the Śiva-tattva, one should perceive sixteen [units] beginning with *ga* and ending with *na*.
4.17cd: O beautiful one, these are the kalās, the words, the mantras, and the worlds.
4.18ab: They are to be understood as before, according to the specific divisions of their respective numbers.

4.18cd: Listen now to how [the mantras] are divided according to the three branches of knowledge (*vidyā*). 4.19ab: In the partless (*niṣkala*) [form], there is one syllable as a single word, then two [syllables] consisting of one and three syllables.
4.19cd: But in the part-possessing (*sakala*) [form], one should know five [syllables]; in the two [others], there are two sets of one syllable.
4.20ab: Two [mantras] of four and one syllable are considered for the triad beginning with Māyā;
4.20cd: One of four syllables is considered for the dyad beginning with Kāla.
4.21ab: A two-syllabled [mantra] is prescribed for Rañjaka, while a three-syllabled one is desired for Pradhāna.
4.21cd: In the *buddhi*, by means of the pervasion of the eight deities, a two-syllable *pada* is intended.
4.22ab: Thereafter, by means of the pervasion of five groups of eight, there are [the *vidyā* *padas*] consisting of two, one, two, and two syllables respectively.
4.22cd: These are the four *vidyā* *padas*, while the fifth consists of one and a half syllables.
4.23ab: In the earthly principle (tattva), however, there are three [syllables] consisting of one and a half letters each;
4.23cd: and in the limb of Parā, all else—the phonemes, mantras, kalās, and so forth.
4.24ab: Two cosmic eggs (aṇḍas) are pervaded by [Parā] with one and a half [units], while the other two are pervaded separately by [the other goddesses] one by one.
4.24cd: This pervasion of Aparā has been declared in reverse order. 4.25ab: The three eggs are pervaded by the letter *sa*, and the fourth by the trident (*triśūla*).
4.25cd: That which transcends all is pervaded by the emission (*visarga*); this is declared to be the pervasion of Parā.
4.26ab: All this should be fully understood by the yogin who desires his own welfare; 4.26cd: whether for himself or for others, it cannot be attained otherwise.
4.27ab: O Daughter of Śaṅkara, only two are to be known as bestowers of liberation: the man of knowledge and the yogin.
4.27cd: In that regard, those who desire the fruit should understand [the distinction] through their differentiation.
4.28ab: Knowledge is said to be threefold; among these, the first is held to be that consisting of hearing (*śruta*).
4.28cd: Another consists of reflection (*cintā*), and yet another indeed consists of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
4.29ab: The thorough comprehension of the meaning of the treatise is considered the learning of one who is focused.
4.29cd: "This is here, this is there; this is applicable in this context. 4.30ab: Having reflected upon the entire meaning of the treatise as it is systematically established.
4.30cd: Likewise, knowledge consisting of reflection is taught to be of two kinds;

4.31ab: distinguished by being either weak or well-practiced. Among these, that which is well-practiced is described as follows: 4.31cd: When that [knowledge] has been thoroughly perfected, there arises knowledge consisting of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).
4.32ab: Since, by attaining yoga, the yogi obtains the fruit of yoga;
4.32cd: thus, according to the distinction of their realization, the man of knowledge (jñānin) is said to be of four kinds:
4.33ab: the one who has attained, the one who is striving, the accomplished, and otherwise, the most accomplished.
4.33cd: O Goddess, the yogi is of four kinds, as he practices accordingly. 4.34ab: Yoga is declared to be threefold, according to the description of the modes of immersion (*samāveśa*).
4.34cd: Among these, the one who has received the instruction through the lineage succession (*pāramparyakrama*) is [the first].

4.35ab: He who has attained yoga should be known by the wise as being of three kinds; 4.35cd: [The first is] the repeated rejoining of the mind when it has strayed from reality. 4.36ab: The wise desire him who performs this [rejoining] to be one who is striving (ghaṭamāna).
4.36cd: That alone he grasps with his mind, and nothing else, as a second;
4.37ab: then he should be known as one perfected in yoga by those who seek the fruit of yoga. 4.37cd: But he who, wherever he may be situated and however he may act, remains [in that state]—
4.38ab: While enjoying the fruit thereof, he is by no means deprived of it.
4.38cd: He should be known as perfectly accomplished (susiddha), equal to Sadāśiva, O Dear One. 4.39ab: The progressive superiority of these [categories] has thus been declared.
4.39cd: Between the two—the man of knowledge and the yogi—the knower of yoga is superior.

4.40ab: For he possesses knowledge as well, whereas the former is devoid of the fruit of yoga. 4.40cd: And because one who has thoroughly practiced knowledge is declared by the wise to be the giver of liberation.
4.41ab: All this has been told, which is to be known as honored by yogins; 4.41cd: having summarized the meaning of the tantra, [it is] for the benefit of yogins in brief.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the illustrious *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*.
Now begins the fifth chapter: 5.1ab: Now, therefore, O Īśvarī, I shall fully explain the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan).
5.1cd: First, the world of Kālāgni must be purified with diligent effort.
5.2ab: Avīci, Kumbhīpāka, and Raurava as the third;
5.2cd: in the pure realm of the Kūṣmāṇḍas, all are purified—of this there is no doubt.
5.3ab: Beyond that are the seven netherworlds (pātālas); at their beginning is Mahātala.
5.3cd: Then there is Rasātala, and beyond that is Talātala;
5.4ab: Sutala, Nitala, Vitala, and Talātala as well.
5.4cd: By means of pure hāṭaka, the purification of all these is intended.

5.5ab: Above that, the earth is to be known as consisting of seven continents and oceans; 5.5cd: Mount Meru, the abode of the gods, is situated in its center. 5.6ab: Above the earth is the Bhuvarloka, and above that is the Svarloka.
5.6cd: Mahas, Janas, Tapas, and Satya—this is the sevenfold world. 5.7ab: It is therein that the fourteen-fold collection of living beings proceeds.
5.7cd: The immobile, the serpent species, and likewise the bird species.
5.8ab: That which is known as Mṛga, that called Paśu, the fifth, and another, the Mānuṣa;
5.8cd: the Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yākṣa, Gāndharva, and Aindra;
5.9ab: the Saumya, the Prājāpatya, and the Brāhma—these are the fourteen here.
5.9cd: When this Brahma-world has been completely purified, there is the purification of all this [else]. 5.10ab: After that comes the world of Viṣṇu, and immediately following that is my own world.
5.10cd: When that is purified, all of this becomes pure; of this there is no doubt.
5.11ab: O Dear One, by these five worlds beginning with Kālāgni, which are pure, 5.11cd: all this situated within the Brahmāṇḍa is purified. 5.12ab:
Outside of that are the separate worlds of the hundred Rudras.
5.12cd: One should subsequently purify ten [deities], and one [deity] surrounded by their leaders.
5.13ab: Ananta is the first among them, and Kapālīśa is another.
5.13cd: Agnirudra, Yama, Nairṛta, and Bala as well.
5.14ab: Śīghra, Nidhīśvara, and another, Sarvavidyādhipa;
5.14cd: Śambhu, Vīrabhadra, and Vidhūmajvalanaprabha— 5.15ab: By these eleven pure ones, the hundred is considered pure.
5.15cd: Above them, in front, eight [sites] are established in groups of five.
5.16ab: Lakulī, Bhārabhūti, Diṇḍi, Āṣāḍhi, and Puṣkara; 5.16cd: Naimiṣa, Prabhāsa, and Amareśa—this is the group of eight.
5.17ab: This has been declared as pertaining to each individual self; therefore, it is more secret than the secret.
5.17cd: Therein are Bhairava, Kedāra, and Mahākāla, together with Madhyama. 5.18ab: [Also] Āmrātikeśa, Jalpeśa, Śrīśaila, along with Harīndu.
5.18cd: Bhīmeśvara, Mahendra, Aṭṭahāsa, along with Vimaleśvara; 5.19ab: Kanakhala, Nākhala, Kurukṣetra, and likewise Gayā.
5.19cd: This third secret [set] is now declared to be purifying.

5.20ab: Sthānu and Svarṇākṣaka are the first two; Bhadra and Gokarṇaka are the next two. 5.20cd: [Then] Mahākāla, Avimukteśa, Rudrakoṭi, Ambara, and Āpada. 5.21ab: Sthūla, Sthūleśvara, Śaṅkukarṇa, and Kālañjara as well.
5.21cd: Maṇḍaleśvara, Mākoṭa, Diraṇḍa, and Chagalāṇḍaka;

5.22ab: these are declared as the eight Sthāṇus, situated up to the level of the ego (ahaṅkāra). 5.22cd: Listen as I describe the eight classes of divine beings (devayoni) residing in the intellect (buddhi).

5.23ab: The Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yākṣa, Gāndharva, and Aindra [marriages], 5.23cd: as well as the Saumya, the Prājāpatya, and the Brāhma is desired as the eighth. 5.24ab: Among these, however, the eightfold yoga is primary; therein, at the outset, the uncreated (akṛta) occurs.
5.24cd: And [the kalpas] Kṛta, Raibhava, Brāhma, and immediately after that Vaiṣṇava; 5.25ab: Kaumāra, Auma, and Śraikaṇṭha—thus is the eightfold yoga. 5.25cd:
[The kalpas] Puruṣa, Vāma, Abhīma, Ugra, Bhava, Īśāna, and Ekavīraka.
5.26ab: Pracaṇḍa, Umādhava, and Aja, as well as Ananta and Ekaśiva; 5.26cd: Krodheśa and Caṇḍa [are in] Vidyā, and Saṃvarta and Jyotis indeed [are in] Kalā.
5.27ab: Surapañcāntaka and Para are to be known in the principle (tattva) of Kalā.
5.27cd: Ekavīra, Śikhaṇḍīśa, and Śrīkaṇṭha have resorted to Kāla.
5.28ab: Those beginning with Mahātejas are known as the lords of the maṇḍalas. 5.28cd: Vāmadeva and Bhavodbhava are situated there in the Māyā-tattva.
5.29ab: Ekapiṅga, Īkṣaṇa, Īśāna, Bhuvaneśa, and Purassara; 5.29cd: accompanied by Aṅguṣṭhamātra, they possess a splendor equal to the fire of cosmic destruction.
5.30ab: The wise say that there are also five worlds within the Vidyātattva.
5.30cd: Among them, Hālāhala is the first, and Rudra is the other, Krodha.
5.31ab: Ambikā, Aghorā, and Vāmadevī are proclaimed. 5.31cd: In the case of Īśvara, the Maheśvaras begin with Pibanā and end with Aghorā.
5.32ab: Raudrī, Jyeṣṭhā, Vāmā, as well as Śakti and Sadāśiva— 5.32cd: The wise know these to be the five worlds within the Sakala [tattva].
5.33ab: Thus, across all the tattvas, there are one hundred and eighteen [worlds].
5.33cd: The worlds are to be fully understood in brief, and not in detail. 5.34ab: By means of this purity, all things are purified; of this there is no doubt.
5.34cd: For when the purification of all paths is to be accomplished, one must possess great intelligence.

5.35ab: Having purified everything up to the limit, one should contemplate union within Śivā. 5.35cd: The knower of yoga, having meditated upon the manifest (sakala) for the sake of one who desires enjoyment, should perform yoga.
5.36ab: Thus has this path called "the worlds" been proclaimed according to my own view.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*.
Now begins the sixth chapter, "The Path of the Body" (Dehamārgādhikāra).
6.1ab: Now, [we shall explain] how this collection of entities is established within the body.

6.1cd: It is performed during the initiations of knowledge; thus it is now being declared. 6.2ab: One should place the five elements below the feet with a pervasion of two finger-breadths. 6.2cd: And the earth-principle up to the ankles, and then the [other] elements beginning with water in their proper order.
6.3ab: Likewise, above the navel, one should contemplate the group of six principles ending with the conclusion of the [six] joints (parva).
6.3cd: One should meditate upon the group of six principles beginning from the principle of the Person (puruṣa-tattva) and ending with the principle of Limited Agency (kalā-tattva).
6.4ab: Then, being well-composed, [one should contemplate] the four principles beginning with Māyā.
6.4cd: One should contemplate all things as ending with the [element] of space through a pervasion extending four finger-breadths.
6.5ab: Thereafter, one should contemplate the Śiva-principle, which is of the nature of light and undisturbed.
6.5cd: One should remember it as the pervader of all, both externally and internally.
6.6ab: This deposition (nyāsa) has been proclaimed according to the division of the thirty-six principles (tattvas).
6.6cd: Now, the five principles are described as they exist within the body. 6.7ab: From the navel upwards, there are six joints in successive order.
6.7cd: The earth principle (dharātattva) pervades up to the ankles; the remainder here is pervaded by water.
6.8ab: Above that, there are twenty-two joints, which are enveloped by fire.
6.8cd: From there, twelve joints are declared to be the pervasion of air.
6.9ab: One should contemplate that which extends to the limit of space, supreme and tranquil, pervading all things.
6.9cd: This same [contemplation] is prescribed even in the ritual procedures for the five sections beginning with Śakti.
6.10ab: In the Trikaṇḍa system, the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) is declared to extend up to the throat.
6.10cd: Above that is the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), and the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) is as before.
6.11ab: Thus the rule of the principles has been declared; now the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan) is likewise described.
6.11cd: From Kālāgni up to Vīrabhadra, there are sixteen cities (pura).
6.12ab: Having meditated, one should place [the mantras] in due order, ending at the ankles, according to the rule.
6.12cd: From there, extending by one finger-breadth each in succession, starting from Lakulīśa;
6.13ab: one should place [the mantras] ending with Dviraṇḍa, and Chagalāṇḍaka occupies three finger-breadths.
6.13cd: Then, by the extension of the big toe, one should contemplate the eight deities of yoga individually.
6.14ab: Thereafter, by the extension of half a finger-breadth, one should contemplate the six cities in sequence.
6.14cd: One should contemplate a group of four in two [locations], and one [deity] in another single location.
6.15ab: In the triad beginning with Vidyā, there are two and one divisions respectively according to the sequence starting from the North.
6.15cd: In the [division of] Time, each one is indicated individually in due order.
6.16ab: The pervasion (vyāpti) of the lords of the maṇḍalas is considered to be half a finger-breadth (ardhāṅgula).
6.16cd: Above that, for a triad [of notes], there is what is called a parvan deficient by one-third;
6.17ab: and for a dyad, it is complete, and is declared to be a pentad (pañcaka).
6.17cd: One should likewise recognize another as an octad (aṣṭaka) and a pentad.
6.18ab: In this procedure for the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), one should contemplate Śiva as previously described.
6.18cd: Here, the *padas* are of two kinds, distinguished by their division into *vargas* and *vidyās*.
6.19ab: Their pervasion (*vyāpti*) is like that of those mantras; listen now to how it is so.
6.19cd: The first [band] is four finger-breadths wide, while the other two are each eight finger-breadths.
6.20ab: From this point, three are ten finger-breadths, and one is fifteen finger-breadths. 6.20cd: Another is four finger-breadths wider, and the great ninth is all-pervasive.
6.21ab: In the division consisting of nineteen parts, the pervasion is now described.
6.21cd: Each [subsequent part] should be known as two finger-breadths; among them, the first three parts [are as follows].
6.22ab: Four [parts] are eight finger-breadths each, and beyond that, one is ten finger-breadths.
6.22cd: Two [units] are two finger-breadths (dvyaṅgula), and the other two feet are six finger-breadths (ṣaḍaṅgula) beyond that.
6.23ab: Another is twelve finger-breadths, and the other two are each five finger-breadths.
6.23cd: Two feet consist of four joints (catuṣparva), and likewise the other two consist of two joints (dviparvaṇī).
6.24ab: Another pervasive *pada* has been proclaimed as being like the previous one;
6.24cd: this other procedure has been taught; now hear [the description of] the *parāpara*.
6.25ab: Like the previous one, the earth element (*pṛthivītattva*) is to be known as four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*).
6.25cd: One should mark the [sections] ending with Dhiṣaṇa as measuring two and a half finger-breadths each;
6.26ab: Pradhāna is to be known as three finger-breadths; one should indicate the remainder as before.
6.26cd: In the other [section] also, as before, Pṛthvī is [three finger-breadths], and the others are likewise.
6.27ab: One should rely on the four-jointed *pradhāna* as before for the remainder.
6.27cd: For although the letters are of two kinds, their division is said to be sixfold.
6.28ab: It is to be known in its ultimate sense through the method of the path of reality (*tattvamārga*).

6.28cd: According to the preceding sūtras, one should establish the triadic nature of the *pada*, mantra, *kalā*, and so forth; 6.29ab: following the path described for the principles (*tattva*) and phonemes (*varṇa*).
6.29cd: Thus, for the body of the elemental being (*bhūtaśarīra*), by means of the Guru who is the very form of Śiva,
6.30ab: "Initiation, which bestows all fruits, must be performed according to the prescribed rule.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, on the Path of the Body, in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*.
[Now begins] the seventh chapter, on Mudrās.
7.1ab: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the powers of Śiva known as mudrās;
7.1cd: protected by which the practitioner of mantra attains the perfection of mantra.
7.2ab: The trident, and likewise the lotus, the spear, the discus together with the thunderbolt—
7.2cd: Daṇḍadaṃṣṭra, Mahāpreta, Mahāmudrā, and Khageśvarī;

7.3ab: Mahodayā and Karālā, as well as the khaṭvāṅga together with the skull-cup (kapāla); 7.3cd: the plow (hala), the noose (pāśa), the goad (aṅkuśa), the bell (ghaṇṭā), the mallet (mudgara), and another [weapon] with three points (triśikha).
7.4ab: Invocation, installation, and retention, as well as the offering of substances and prostration— 7.4cd: these, O Goddess worshipped by heroes, should be known as the Amṛtā Yoga-mudrā.
7.5ab: The index, middle, and ring fingers of the right hand are extended.
7.5cd: When the little finger and the thumb are pressed together, it is proclaimed as the trident (triśūla) mudrā.
7.6ab: Having formed the hands in the shape of a lotus, one should display the lotus (padma) mudrā.
7.6cd: Having extended the two hands facing each other with the fingers interlaced.

7.7ab: When the middle finger is extended at the base of the palm, it is held to be the *śakti* of Kaumārī. 7.7cd: But from the upturned left fist, [the right hand]— 7.8ab: Should cast the fist; this is the *cakra*, beloved of Nārāyaṇī.
7.8cd: One should place the right hand, facing downwards, above the left hand, which is turned upwards.
7.9ab: The little finger and the thumb are joined together, while the remaining fingers rest against the wrists.
7.9cd: This is renowned as the Vajra-mudrā; it brings satisfaction to Indra.
7.10ab: The right fist, extended upward with the thumb placed inside, 7.10cd:
is renowned as the *daṇḍamudrā*, beloved by the family of Vaivasvata.
7.11ab: One should bring the little finger of the left fist toward the mouth.
7.11cd: O Goddess, this is proclaimed as Daṃṣṭrā, the delighter of the Cāmuṇḍā family.
7.12ab: The left knee is bent, while the two hands hang down along the back.
7.12cd: The eyes are distorted, the neck is broken, and the tongue is protruded.
7.13ab: Yogīśvarī is considered the beloved of the entire host of yogis and is regarded as a preta.
7.13cd: The wise one should lead the two hands, facing downward, from the feet to the heart.
7.14ab: One should lead them upward, facing each other, from the side of the face to above.
7.14cd: She is renowned as Mahāmudrā in the practice of purifying the body.
7.15ab: And she performs all actions for the sake of the yogis' attainment of yoga.
7.15cd: Having assumed the lotus posture, the yogi should place Akṣeśvara at the navel.
7.16ab: One should lead that [wind] in the form of a staff as far as the three voids (kha). 7.16cd: Having restrained it there, one should quickly impel it through the three voids.
7.17ab: Having bound this, the great hero attains movement in the sky.
7.17cd: Of the right hand facing downwards, the left [hand] is turned upwards above it.
7.18ab: One should press its ring finger and middle finger with the left thumb.
7.18cd: [One should press] its little finger with the index finger, and the index finger with the little finger.
7.19ab: One should press the thumb with the middle and ring fingers;
7.19cd: this mudrā is called Mahodayā, which brings about great prosperity for men. 7.20ab: With the ring and little fingers, one should part the corners of the mouth.
7.20cd: The mantra-practitioner should lick his tongue and cause a cry of "hā hā" to be made.
7.21ab: With a wrathful gaze, this fierce mudrā causes terror to the wicked.
7.21cd: The left fist is placed upon the left shoulder with the index finger raised.
7.22ab: The mudrā known as Khaṭvāṅga has been described; now hear about the Kapāla. 7.22cd: The palm of the right hand is hollowed out with the fingers slightly contracted.
7.23ab: This should be known as the Kapāla; now the Hala is being described.
7.23cd: When the right fist is clenched and the index finger of the left fist [is extended], 7.24ab:
and that index finger is grasped by the curved index finger [of the right hand], it is proclaimed as the *halamudrā*.
7.24cd: With the two fists placed behind, the two index fingers of the right and left [hands] [are extended].
7.25ab: The noose is formed by the left thumb-tip joined to [the index finger], with the hand extended and slightly curved.
7.25cd: As is the left fist in the plow gesture (*hala*), so is the goad (*aṅkuśa*) when the right hand is absent.
7.26ab: When the left hand is positioned face-down, the wise one [should place] the right index finger [upon it].

7.26cd: One should move the bell situated in the middle; this is considered the beloved Ghaṇṭāmudrā. 7.27ab: The two hands should be turned upward with the fingers interlaced one within the other. 7.27cd: The two ring fingers should rest on the back of the middle fingers, and the two index fingers should be placed upon the root joints [of the ring fingers].
The two middle fingers should be joined up to the fingertips, while the two little fingers are held apart.
The index fingers are positioned on the sides of the middle fingers and kept slightly separated;
this is indeed the "Three-Pointed Hammer" (*mudgara*), which brings about possession in an instant.

7.29cd: Having formed the *añjali* with both hands, the wise one should place the thumbs at the base joints of the ring fingers during the rite of mantra-invocation. 7.30ab: [The same] should be arranged by the learned practitioner for the ritual of invocation. 7.30cd: Two fists with the thumbs raised are proclaimed as the *sthāpanī* (the mudrā of installation).
7.31ab: Only the two thumbs placed within the palms are to be known as the *saṃnirodhinī* [mudrā].
7.31cd: But the *dravyadā* is declared here to be the *saṃmukhī*.
7.32ab: With the hands joined face-to-face at the heart, the fingers are extended.
7.32cd: This salutation is the mudrā for the ritual of bowing to the mantra.
7.33ab: All the fingers of both hands are positioned with each interlaced with the other. 7.33cd: One should place the right little finger upon the tip of the left ring finger.
7.34ab: Likewise, the right [hand] and the left, with the index and middle fingers likewise [joined];
7.34cd: With the two thumbs placed at the base of the middle fingers—this is the *amṛtaprabhā* mudrā.
7.35ab: The right [hand] is positioned at the base of the navel, resting upon the left.
7.35cd: For the rite of yoga, the index finger and thumb are joined and raised.
7.36ab: In this manner, the wise practitioner of mantra should bind the collection of mudrās at his heart.
7.36cd: The expressive mantras for all of these are: *oṃ hrīṃ* [insert name] *namaḥ*.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the Section on Mudrās, in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sacrifice that grants all desires,
by the mere sight of which one becomes esteemed by the Yoginīs.

8.2ab: Therein, first, one should cause a delightful sacrificial ground to be made in an auspicious field, 8.2cd: provided with a circular fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa) [measuring] twenty-five finger-breadths all around, with its navel [the center] measuring half of that. 8.3ab: [The pit should be] surrounded by a rim of twenty-five finger-breadths.
8.3cd: Even with a single lock of hair, he is beautiful with lips like the [new] moon’s crescent.
8.4ab: Then, having bathed and conquered the pairs of opposites, the knower of mantras performs the bath of being (bhāva-snāna).
8.4cd: And that is declared to be of six kinds, in the sequence beginning with the ash-bath (bhasma-snāna).
8.5ab: Having consecrated the ashes seven times with the Great Weapon mantra, [one performs] the ash-bath.
8.5cd: For the sake of cleansing impurities, one should dust the body according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
8.6ab: Afterwards, one should veil [the body] starting from the head with the five limbs of the Vidyā.
8.6cd: One should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) with the root mantra itself, accompanied by the six limbs.
8.7ab: Then, whether unclothed or well-clothed, one should wash both hands and feet.
8.7cd: Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should perform the purification (mārjana) with the Vidyā consisting of many syllables.
8.8ab: Having performed the general *nyāsa*, one should recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* with the second [mantra].
8.8cd: One should perform the worship (*upasthāna*) with the *mālinī* and recite the supreme single-syllable [mantra].
8.9ab: Even during a water-bath, one should take earth consecrated seven times with the *astra* [mantra].
8.9cd: Having touched the body as before, one should perform the bath for removing impurities.
8.10ab: And here, the ritual bath and so forth are performed as before, but with water.
8.10cd: Having performed the common ritual bath, [the practitioner] consecrates [himself] with the mantras of the three Vidyās.
8.11ab: One who knows the mantra should sprinkle water upon the head for the purpose of the mantra-bath.
8.11cd: One should perform the Vāyavya bath using dust raised by a cow’s hoof. 8.12ab: Reciting the Great Weapon (Mahāstra) mantra, one should proceed seven steps while absorbed in meditation.
8.12cd: That very [liquid] may return again by recollecting the higher and the lower.
8.13ab: Even that which is divine is considered to be of such a nature through the conjunction of rain and heat.
8.13cd: However, in that case, the mantra-practitioner should visualize the supreme river flowing with nectar.
8.14ab: Having raised fire from the base of the thumb with the *astra* mantra, one should burn [it away].
8.14cd: Afterwards, one should flood one’s own body with the supreme nectar (*amṛta*).
8.15ab: Having taken up the mantra from the sun and so forth, one should go while recollecting the *astra*.

8.15cd: Purified by the weapon-mantra, one should enter the sacrificial hall, pure and undisturbed. 8.16ab: Having worshipped the guardians of the door there, and having meditated, one should cast a flower consecrated with the Great Weapon-mantra for the pacification of blazing obstacles.
8.17ab: Then, having performed the visualization of protection with the weapon-mantra in all ten directions, 8.17cd:

one should enter the sacrificial hall, which is joined with fire like the Fire-god himself. 8.18ab: Facing either the east or the north, one should begin the specific ritual placement (*viśeṣanyāsa*).
8.18cd: Therein, first, with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), which possesses a brilliance equal to the fire of time (*kālānala*), 8.19ab:
one should visualize the body, burnt from the tip of the big toe, together with its exterior and interior.
8.19cd: Having meditated upon that ash being scattered by the wind of the armor-mantra (*kavaca*),...
8.20ab: One should contemplate the Self as having the form of a drop of Śiva.
8.20cd: Then, one who is invincible should unite the Power [Śakti] with it, thinking "I am He.
8.21ab: Thereafter, O Consort of Śaṅkara, one should meditate upon the embodiment of the Vidyā by means of this mantra.
8.21cd: [The letter] *da* is marked by a staff (*daṇḍākrānta*), possesses great vital breath (*mahāprāṇa*), and is mounted upon a staff (*daṇḍārūḍha*) with its navel.
8.22ab: Below that is the hip (*nitamba*), and below that again is the left breast (*vāmastana*).
8.22cd: Then the throat (*kaṇṭha*) and the left peak (*vāmaśikhara*), adorned with the left seal (*vāmamudrā*).
8.23ab: A dot, a half-moon, and a sky [the letter *ha*], adorned with *nāda*, *śakti*, and a dot;
8.23cd: This, O Goddess, is the *piṇḍa* known as the Ninefold (*navātmaka*).
8.24ab: It brings about all accomplishments and is proclaimed along with its secret.
8.24cd: This [mantra], deprived of three syllables at the end and joined with the six long vowels, 8.25ab:
one should fashion the six limbs, beginning with the heart, according to the distinction of the *jātis*.
8.25cd: And by means of the seeds *kṣaya-ra-vala*, which are radiant and adorned with the nasal drop (*bindu*).
8.26ab: One should first fashion the faces in sequence, beginning with the upward-facing one.
8.26cd: Then, for the sake of accomplishing the procedure for the individual limbs, one should assign [the syllables] to the forehead and so forth.
8.27ab: One should assign the letter *a* to the forehead and the second [vowel] to the face.
Having placed *i* and *ī* on the two eyes, one should assign *u* and *ū* to the two ears.
Likewise, one should place *ṛ* and *ṝ* on the two nostrils, and similarly *ḷ* and *ḹ* on the two cheeks.
One should place *e* and *ai* on the lower and upper teeth, and likewise *o* and *au* on the two lips.

8.29ab: One should fashion the letter *aṃ* with the visarga for the crest-lock and for the tongue. 8.29cd: And one should place the *ka*-group on the right shoulder, the arm, the hand, and the fingers and nails. 8.30ab: Likewise, one should place [the *ca*-group] on the left in the same sequence, beginning with the first [letter].
8.30cd: One should place the two groups beginning with *ṭa* and *ta*, as before, upon the hips, the thighs, and so forth.
8.31ab: One should place [the letters] in sequence on the two sides, the back, the belly, and the heart.
8.31cd: One should assign the group beginning with *ya* to the skin, blood, flesh, and sinews.
8.32ab: In cases of affliction of the bones, marrow, semen, or the vital breaths, one should perform the fivefold [rite].
8.32cd: Then, having assigned the limbs of the form, the wise one should invoke Śiva.
8.33ab: One should place the navel above the vital breath, and above that, the right finger.
8.33cd: Flowing from the left ear, Śiva bestows all accomplishments.
8.34ab: For this is the supreme true nature of the great-souled Bhairava.
8.34cd: By means of this, the limbs [of the mantra] should be performed as before, according to the differentiation of the vowels.
8.35ab: The Mūrtinyāsa consists of the emanation and the three principles (tritattva), along with the eight forms together with their limbs.
8.35cd: Śiva, together with his limbs, constitutes the sixfold placement; this is what is proclaimed as the Nyāsa.
8.36ab: After that, one should perform the Śākta Nyāsa upon this; listen to it as it is told.
8.36cd: Having deposited Parāparā upon the form (mūrti) and her faces, as well as Mālinī;
8.37ab: One should subsequently deposit the triad beginning with Parā on the crest, the heart, and the feet.
8.37cd: [One should deposit] in sequence on the head, face, throat, heart, navel, secret place, thighs, and feet.
8.38ab: Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the eight [mantras] beginning with Aghorī, one should perform the placement of the limbs of the Vidyā as before.
8.38cd: Then, one should invoke the Śakti, who is saluted by all yogis.
8.39ab: The individual soul (*jīva*), situated within the cavity of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), possesses a radiance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction (*kālānala*).
8.39cd: But [the syllable] *atidīpta* is adorned with the left foot and a *bindu* on its head; 8.40ab: joined with the right knee, it is accompanied by the entire host of Mothers.
8.40cd: Satisfied by this, they all grant the desired fruit.
8.41ab: For this is declared to be the supreme state of being for Mothers.
8.41cd: Therefore, the practitioner of mantra should recite this if he desires the highest accomplishment.
8.42ab: The immersion into the power of Rudra is eternally established herein.
8.42cd: Because this supreme power (parā-śakti) is proclaimed through this differentiation;
8.43ab: whatever accomplishments (siddhi) exist in the Tantra, they are all brought about by her.
8.43cd: One should fashion her limbs as before, according to the distinction of the vowels.
8.44ab: The Form (mūrti) together with its faces, the Power (śakti), and the triad of Vidyās; 8.44cd: And the group of eight beginning with Aghorī, as well as the five limbs of the Vidyā;
8.45ab: And the Supreme Power (parā śakti) along with her limbs—this is declared to be the sixfold ritual deposition (nyāsa).
8.45cd: Therefore, this *yāmala* deposition (*nyāsa*) is for the sake of attaining all accomplishments (*siddhi*).

8.46ab: Or rather, this left-hand (*vāma*) procedure should be performed by those who rely on the path of liberation (*mukti*). 8.46cd: Or it may be done separately according to the distinction between phonemes (*varṇa*) and mantras by those who desire those specific fruits.

8.47ab: As many as have been enumerated through their various divisions as designations for Śambhu, Śakti, and the individual soul (aṇu), 8.47cd: even among those, this fivefold deposition (nyāsa) is considered to be exactly the same.
8.48ab: However, whichever [deity] is external in a particular case, that [deity] there is accompanied by the limbs (aṅga).
8.48cd: "The sixth [element] should be present"—thus it is everywhere declared that this [sacrifice] consists of six parts.

8.49ab: Without contradicting one's own established practice, through conceptualizations of existence and non-existence, 8.49cd: all sacrificial materials should be prepared according to the rules by the wise.

8.50ab: Then, having taken the vessel for the *argha* offering—which is conceptually purified of both existence and non-existence— 8.50cd: and which has been burnt by the fire of the weapon-mantra and drenched with the water of power, it becomes pure.
8.51ab: This same purification should be performed for whatever other object is present here.
8.51cd: By this very path, one who possesses discernment should act.
8.52ab: One should not conceptualize any object here that has not been purified.
8.52cd: Therefore, everything is pure; even that which is impure is pure.
8.53ab: Having filled that [vessel] with water and offered it with the six limbs, 8.53cd: and having rendered all substances immortal, one should purify them with that [water].
8.54ab: But having worshipped oneself, one should perform the internal rite as follows.
8.54cd: Thus I shall describe it to you, O you who are honored by the assembly of all yogis.
8.55ab: First, at the very beginning, there is the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti), four finger-breadths below the navel.
8.55cd: The quartet consists of the earth, the ocean, the boat, and the bulb (kanda).
8.56ab: Each finger-breadth (aṅgula) of this [shaft] shall constitute the *amalasaraka* of the trident (*śūla*). 8.56cd: Beyond that, one should fashion for it a shaft (*daṇḍa*) called the *ananta*.
8.57ab: Here, from the point of the *lambikā* upwards, a knot (*granthi*) is prescribed above the trident.
8.57cd: O Great Goddess, without piercing this great ocean of the snare-net, 8.58ab: that human being does not attain union with Śiva;
8.58cd: [namely] the fourfold [powers]: dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty.
8.59ab: The practitioner of mantra should contemplate [the four limbs] in the corners, starting from the southeast (āgneya) in due order;
8.59cd: and one should remember the quartet of limbs in the directions, beginning with the east.
8.60ab: Above the knot and below the trident, there must be a quadrangular space (catuṣkikā).
8.60cd: They say that very same thing is the *vidyātattva*, conjoined with the three coverings (*chadana*).
8.61ab: One should contemplate that *tattva* between the *kaka* and the *lambikā*.
8.61cd: The wise one should contemplate the *kakhatattva*, which has the form of a lotus, as belonging to Īśvara.
8.62ab: [One should visualize] the white [lotus], fully blossomed, complete with its pericarp and filaments, and endowed with the seed-syllable.
8.62cd: Subsequently, one should install the nine [shaktis] beginning with Vāmā, starting from the eastern petal.
8.63ab: These are Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, and likewise Parā.
8.63cd: And likewise Kalavikaraṇī and Balavikaraṇī; 8.64ab: Another is Balapramathanī, and also Sarvabhūtadamanī;
8.64cd: And Manonmanī one should place in the middle, along the path of the sun.
8.65ab: One should also conceive another ninefold group, beginning with Vibhu, in reverse order.
8.65cd: [These are] Vibhu, Jñānin, Kriyā, Icchā, Vāgīśī, and likewise Jvālinī; 8.66ab: Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—all of them possessing the radiance of the fire of time (kālānala).
8.66cd: Those who were previously established as Śākta—namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara—are the lords residing within the petals, filaments, and centers of the mandalas. 8.67cd:
One should contemplate the resonance (dhvani) of the sun, moon, and fire as being known by those names.

8.68ab: And one should meditate on the conscious Lord Mahāpreta, laughing, with a body like ten million fires of cosmic destruction; such is the entire seat. 8.69ab: One should remember the three-pronged trident of power (śakti-śūla) arisen from his navel.
8.69cd: One should contemplate that which has emerged from the three *ka-kha* [phonemes] and terminates at the limit of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*).
8.70ab: Then, one should contemplate a triad of lotuses belonging to Śakti upon its prongs.
8.70cd: White and the presiding authority over all—this is the supreme seat (*paramāsana*).
8.71ab: Thereupon, one should contemplate above that the form known as Vidyā;

8.71cd: and then the one called Ātman within it, together with the previously mentioned installation consisting of Śiva. 8.72ab: Then, in the center, the supreme Śakti, and in the two directions of south and north, the pair.
8.72cd: Having meditated upon Parāparā, who by her very nature is red in color and possesses great power, 8.73ab: who assumes forms at will, slightly fierce yet not terrifying;
8.73cd: and [meditated upon] Aparā on the left horn, who is terrifying and dark-brown in hue.
One should meditate upon the Goddess who assumes forms at will, who destroys the suffering of those who bow before her,
the supreme Goddess who nourishes all, and whose radiance is like ten million times ten thousand moons;
one should contemplate her even when the sixfold Śākta ritual has been performed, as well as in the case of the [six] forms and so forth.

8.75cd: One should subsequently place the five ancillaries of the Vidyā in the directions beginning with the southeast (āgneyī). 8.76ab: [One should place them] in the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, and in the south, respectively.
8.76cd: In that same manner, according to the prescribed rule, one should contemplate the ancillaries of Śakti and the ancillaries of Śiva.

8.77ab: However, one should meditate on the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) in the directions beginning with Indra (the east), and the *locana* [mantra] in the center; 8.77cd: as well as the eight [mantras] beginning with Aghora, accompanied by the eight [deities] beginning with Aghorī. 8.78ab: Since they form an enclosure for all [of these], one should also visualize the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) on the outside.
8.78cd: Having visualized the weapons with their own mantras, one should thereafter commence the recitation (*japa*).
8.79ab: Having become absorbed in that very form, one should contemplate each [weapon] ten times.
8.79cd: Having meditated upon it as resembling a blazing fire, one should utter [the mantra] ending in *svāhā*.

8.80ab: The mantra-practitioner [should offer] once for each [deity] for the successful accomplishment of the fire-sacrifice ritual. 8.80cd: Thus has been described the mental sacrifice (mānasayāga) as a collective whole.
8.81ab: This is declared to be the trident (triśūla), consisting of a single staff and possessing three powers.
8.81cd: O fair-faced one, without understanding this power of the *śakti-śūla* in this way, 8.82ab:

even after binding the *khecarī-mudrā*, one does not fly up from the surface of the earth. 8.82cd: Thus has the *śāmbhava* [state] been described; that which ends with the eighth is intended as the *śākta*.
8.83ab: One should know that the individual (āṇava) [power] extends to the end of the fourth [tattva]; thus is the triad of spikes (śūla) conceived.
8.83cd: By means of a separate ritual procedure for sacrifice, one should meditate upon the wheel of powers (śakticakra).
8.84ab: Having bound the sky-farer (khecarī) by that as well, one thus abandons the surface of the earth.
8.84cd: Then, having consecrated the grains twenty-one times with the Great Weapon mantra (mahāstra), 8.85ab:

one should scatter them in all directions while visualizing them as blazing fire. 8.85cd: Having meditated upon that house as being free from obstacles, one should withdraw [the visualization] and lead it toward the northeast direction.
8.86ab: Then the wise one should prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with the five faces [of the mantra].
8.86cd: These are cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and likewise clarified butter.
8.87ab: He should consecrate the water of kuśa grass with the six-limbed [mantra], ending with the upward-facing [face].
8.87cd: Having formed the *mudrā* of the nectar of substances, one should contemplate its true nature (*tattva*).
