8.88ab: With that [nectar], one should sprinkle the ground; with a small portion, one should set aside the rest.
8.88cd: Then one should perform the *vāstuyāga* by means of the recitation of the *Mālinī*.
8.89ab: Having filled his joined palms with flowers, he should utter the syllables beginning with *pha*.
8.89cd: Having meditated upon the path ending with *śakti*, he should cast it into the end of *na*.
8.90ab: Having offered perfume, incense, and so forth, he should worship Gaṇeśāna.

8.90cd: Having placed the sixfold seat (āsana), then upon that [with] the *praṇava* (OM); 8.91ab: With the mantra "GĀM," one should worship Vighneśa with perfumes, flowers, and so forth. 8.91cd: Its limbs [are worshipped] with the syllable GA, joined with the six long vowels.

8.92ab: Having meditated upon the three-eyed, joyful one who has the face of an elephant and a dwarf-like form, 8.92cd: and having dismissed him, one desiring success should worship the Great Weapon (mahāstra) in due order.
8.93ab: Having likewise bestowed infinity, as well as virtue, knowledge, and dispassion.
8.93cd: Sovereignty and the pericarp—this is the sixfold arising seat.
8.94ab: Upon this, having meditated, one should place [the deity] who bears a sword and a shield.
8.94cd: Terrifying, with great fangs, most fierce, and with a face knit in a frown.
8.95ab: Endowed with the six limbs and surrounded by the Mothers of the Directions;
8.95cd: The six limbs [should be visualized] with their own mantras, illuminated by the syllable *phaṭ*.
8.96ab: Having contemplated that very form, one should then worship the eight Mothers.
8.96cd: One should simultaneously visualize Indrāṇī on the eastern petal, holding a thunderbolt.
8.97ab: Then the wise one [should visualize] Āgneyī with a spear in her hand, and Yāmyā with a staff in her hand. 8.97cd: [He should likewise visualize] Nairṛtī, Varuṇānī, and Vāyavī.
8.98ab: O Dear One, one should contemplate [the goddesses] simultaneously as being equipped with a sword, a noose, and a banner;
8.98cd: the Kauverī holding a mallet in her hand, and the Īśānī joined with a trident.
8.99ab: Having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the independent system (svatantra).
8.99cd: First, one should prepare a water-pot consecrated with more than a thousand recitations of the mantra.
8.100ab: One should perform a fire-oblation (homa) of a thousand [offerings] therein; then, having performed the recitation (japa), one should dismiss [the deity].
8.100cd: Having completed one hundred and eight [recitations], one should thereafter commence the sacrifice (yājana).
8.101ab: There, first, having taken a jar made of gold or other precious materials, free from blemishes;
8.101cd: filled with all mantras and medicinal herbs, and completely filled with fragrant water;
8.102ab: with mango sprouts at its mouth and a white garland and thread around its neck.
8.102cd: Marked with a *rakṣoghna* tilaka and covered with a pair of white garments;
8.103ab: Consecrated one hundred and eight times with the root mantra and worshipped with it; 8.103cd:
The water-pots (*vārdhānī*) are likewise prepared, but they are worshipped with the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
8.104ab: Having offered a seat with scattered offerings (vikira), the wise one [should proceed];
8.104cd: thereafter, he should worship Indra and the other [deities] in their respective directions with the prescribed mantras accompanied by vowels.
8.105ab: Then, he should offer an unbroken stream from the water-vessel (vārdhānī).
8.105cd: Afterward, one should rotate the vase and speak these words to the Lords of the World:
8.106ab: "O Śakra! For the sake of pacifying obstacles in your own direction, 8.106cd:
you must remain vigilant until the completion of the rite, by the command of Śiva."

8.107ab: Having led [the deity] there, one should first place the jar, which has become the embodiment [of the deity], upon the seat. 8.107cd: One should place the water-vessel (vārdhānī) on its southern side.
8.108ab: The knower of mantras, having performed the placement [of the deities] in the jar, beginning from his own form (ātma-mūrti) and ending with the object of worship, [should proceed].
8.108cd: Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should worship this [deity] in the *vārdhānī* vessel.

8.109ab: Having fashioned a mandala with perfumes at the station of Brahmā, the wise practitioner 8.109cd: should there worship the group of six, or the group of three, or even just the single [deity].
8.110ab: The scraping of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), its drawing out [of lines], its pounding, and its smearing;
8.110cd: Likewise, the preparation of the crossroads and the axle-pit, as well as the placement of the thunderbolt (vajra);
8.111ab: And the arrangement of the strewing of kuśa grass, the enclosing sticks, and the seats.

8.111cd: One should perform everything with the Astra-mantra; one should install the Vidyā-mantra as "oṃ hrīṃ. 8.112ab: Having installed Śiva with "oṃ" and worshipped him again twice, 8.112cd: one should bring the Jātavedas fire into a copper vessel or a clay bowl.
8.113ab: Having meditated on it as the semen of Śiva, one should deposit it into the womb of the Vidyā.

8.113cd: Then, one should perform the five invocations (āhutis) with the very limbs of the Vidyā. 8.114ab: By doing so, the entire ritual process beginning with birth (janana) and the rest is considered accomplished.
8.114cd: Having recollected the supreme and the non-supreme, one should again offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

8.115ab: Having fully worshipped the mother of the fire and the father, one should dismiss them. 8.115cd: Then, having lifted up the fire for the purpose of preparing the sacrificial pap (caru) and other offerings, [one proceeds] once more.

8.116ab: Or else, having drawn out the flame of the blazing fire with the left [nostril] by means of the breath, 8.116cd: and having restrained it in the heart, one should cast it back again through the right [nostril].
8.117ab: And one should offer the full oblation as before; this is another procedure for the fire of Śiva.

8.117cd: Having beheld him in the form of Śiva, the practitioner of mantra should gradually effect the internal dissolution (antaḥkṛti) of his own self. 8.118ab: Having performed that internal dissolution, he should then commence the fire sacrifice (homa).
8.118cd: He should satisfy the root mantra with a hundred oblations, and then the six limbs according to the six-limbed ritual.
8.119ab: For the remaining classes of mantras, the libation is performed with exactly one-tenth [of the number].
8.119cd: Then he should cause the disciples—who are pure, bathed, and have fasted—to enter.
8.120ab: Having prostrated before the Lord of the Gods of gods, who is present in the fourfold [mandala] in due order.

8.120cd: One should offer the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and likewise the tooth-stick. 8.121ab: The success of the sacrificial porridge is achieved by those skilled in sacrifice with milk and rice, using the *hṛdaya* mantra.
8.121cd: Then, having performed the *saṃpāta* rite with seven mantras, it is divided into six portions.
8.122ab: For Śiva, the fire, the guru, and the disciple, the water-vessel and the jar are equal [in status].
8.122cd: Thereafter, one should provide a tooth-stick produced from a milk-tree (*kṣīravṛkṣa*).
8.123ab: Its falling toward the east, the north, the northeast, or upward is auspicious.
8.123cd: Otherwise it is inauspicious; even in that case, there should be one hundred and eight burnt offerings (homa).
8.124ab: Then the instructor should perform the external rite in all directions.
8.124cd: With this mantra: *oṃ kṣaḥ kṣaḥ sarvabhūtebhyaḥ svāhā*.
8.125ab: Having sipped water and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), and having worshipped Śaṅkara;
8.125cd: [lacuna] ... being pure in the house;
8.126ab: Having performed the ritual placement for the disciples and especially for oneself.

8.126cd: At dawn, having performed the daily obligatory rites and so forth, one should reflect upon the dream. 8.127ab: One should disclose an auspicious dream to them; if it is inauspicious, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa).
8.127cd: Then, women adorned with fine garments and ornaments [should present] flowers, fruits, and other such offerings.
8.128ab: Crossing over calamities and descending into auspicious regions;
8.128cd: Drinking liquor, decapitation, and eating raw meat;
8.129ab: Direct vision of a deity and likewise being smeared with excrement.
8.129cd: Having seen such an auspicious [dream], one attains the desired success (*siddhi*).
8.130ab: This very same [dream] occurring otherwise is proclaimed as a bad dream (*duḥsvapna*).
8.130cd: [It includes] eating cooked meat, anointing [the body with oil], falling into pits, and so forth.
8.131ab: Having performed the expiation prescribed in the Tantras, he should thereafter undergo the rite for attaining the status of the twice-born.
8.131cd: The wise man should always perform worship of the gods, the fire, the guru, and the Goddess.
8.132ab: Without first offering these things to them, he should not eat anything at all.
8.132cd: One should avoid the property of the gods, the property of the guru, and the property of Caṇḍī.
8.133ab: A knower of mantras should not engage in anything fruitless, even for a moment.
8.133cd: He should be devoted to the practice of yoga, or likewise devoted to the practice of mantra.
8.134ab: Having thus caused [the disciple] to hear these and other pledges (samaya), he should dismiss him.
8.134cd: Then, the bath for the God of gods, as well as for the disciples or for himself, 8.135ab: he should cause to be performed with the Śiva-vessel (śivakumbha), which removes all evil deeds.
8.135cd: Thus, this ritual of the *samaya* has been proclaimed in brief.
This concludes the eighth chapter, the section on the *samaya*, in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara*;
the ninth chapter is the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*) and ritual action (*kriyā*).
9.1ab: Then, when the Guru is to perform the initiation for those who abide by the pledges (samaya), 9.1cd: having first performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*), [lacuna] 9.2ab:
he should first properly stretch the cord toward the eastern direction, and thereafter...
9.2cd: From the center of that, one should mark [the points] at equal intervals toward the east and west.

9.3ab: By means of a cord [stretched] from the eastern to the western [mark], one should mark the north and south. 9.3cd: One should likewise mark those [points] from the western mark and also from the eastern mark.
9.4ab: One should cast a long cord through the center of the fish, from south to north.

9.4cd: Measuring half the size of the intended field, one should mark it evenly from the center toward the cardinal directions. 9.5ab: Likewise, from the points situated in those directions, one should mark the corners in both clockwise and counter-clockwise order.
9.5cd: One should drop the lines upon them for the sake of establishing a square.
9.6ab: On the hand resting on the cord, one should first divide the eastern half.
9.6cd: Having omitted half a cubit from all sides, extending toward the east and north.
9.7ab: One should divide the remainder into parts equal to the *guṇāṅgula* units.
9.7cd: With vertical compartments (*koṣṭaka*) of three *aṅgulas* each, and eightfold divisions horizontally;
9.8ab: having again omitted two parts each on the southern and northern sides.

9.8cd: On both sides of the Brahma-line, starting from the fourth *jīva*-line toward the east; 9.9ab: Two pairs of crescent moons, each measuring half a square (*bhāga*) and one full square (*bhāga*);
9.9cd: Between them, on the third line, on the southern and northern sides.
9.10ab: The wise [artist] should create two crescent moons by means of internal rotation.
9.10cd: One should place another pair of crescent moons at the tips of those two, situated at the vital points of the other.
9.11ab: One should perform an external outward rotation for each of the two pairs of crescent moons.
9.11cd: In the same manner, one should draw [lines] in the Brahmā-square measuring one square and half a square.
9.12ab: Then, at the end of the second square, on both sides of the Brahmā-square, 9.12cd: two lines should be drawn by the wise, extending eastward and equal to one-third of a square.

9.13ab: One should establish two threads, one situated at the upper tip of the single half-moon and joined to the tip of the Brahma-thread. 9.13cd: These two threads are to be drawn for the purpose of establishing the central prong (*madhyaśṛṅga*). 9.14ab: From the *jīva*-thread at the sides of its tip, a thread is placed at an interval of one [unit].
9.14cd: One should draw a line from the corner of the first half-moon segment to the opposite corner.
9.15ab: From the life-line (jīva) of those same two, one should draw [another line] from the corner of the first half-moon.
9.15cd: In that very manner, one should lead the thread for the sake of establishing the pair of horns.
9.16ab: And on the other half of the site, the pillar is two cubits [in height], with five parts concealed.
9.16cd: Two cubits [of its height] consist of five parts, with five pedestals hidden [therein].
9.17ab: The remainder shall be visible, measuring one part in width.
9.17cd: It should be six units wide and four units long, with a clean core at its base. 9.18ab: At its bottom, a root four *aṅgulas* wide is desired, tapering to a sharp point.
9.18cd: One should construct four doors in the cardinal directions of the primary field.
9.19ab: It should be one cubit in length and half of that in width, with the [petals] being equal to that.
9.19cd: One should make it double on the outside; thereafter, listen to how the lotus is to be made. 9.20ab: One should make circles, each measuring one unit, like a square (veda).
9.20cd: Furthermore, there are eight in each of the directions, making sixteen life-lines (*jīvasūtra*) in total.
9.21ab: Again, one should drop [lines] equal in number to those between each pair of [adjacent lines].
9.21cd: Among these, that which stands on the third circle is a rotation equal to the side-life-line.
9.22ab: One should perform this much [preliminary work], and thereafter bring the tip of the living [thread].

9.22cd: Wherever there is an attachment, once that connection has been made firm, 9.23ab: having performed [the rite] there, the minister should lead [the thread] for the sake of establishing the tips of the petals.
9.23cd: On each petal, one should fashion three filaments. 9.24ab: Likewise, the three "horn-lotuses" (śṛṅgakaja) should be made with double the eight finger-breadths [of the petals].
9.24cd: Then the practitioner of mantra should worship it with powders mixed with white [pigments].
9.25ab: Especially with red, black, yellow, and green [threads];
9.25cd: With a yellow-colored *karṇikā* at the base, middle, and tip; 9.26ab: The network of filaments (*kesarajālakam*) should be made white, red, and yellow.
9.26cd: The petals are white in color, together with the *prativāraṇa* (the protective rim).
9.27ab: Likewise, the yellow [square] is four-cornered, equal in extent to half the pericarp on the outside.
9.27cd: Its sides are [colored] white, red, yellow, and black, starting from the southeast in sequence.
9.28ab: It is held that the horns [of the *śūla*] are made with four [colors] and the circle with three;
9.28cd: the handle (*daṇḍa*) should be blue and red, while the *āmalasāraka* part is yellow. 9.29ab: One should make the shaft (*śūla*) red, which was previously described.

9.29cd: Having left four finger-breadths to the east of the rear door, [one should place] the gate. 9.30ab: It may be four-cornered, circular, or oval, and it should be decorated. 9.30cd: It may have one, two, or three stories, being symmetrical, with a water-spout on top, or both.
9.31ab: Adorned with many ornaments such as the primary and secondary embellishments of skulls and necklaces;
9.31cd: Possessing various shapes and forms, and provided with vine-like delicate dwellings;
9.32ab: When it has been thus perfectly completed, its cleaning is performed with scented cloth.
9.32cd: Having performed the ritual bath, one should carry out the rite exactly as previously described.

9.33ab: Having entered as before, the practitioner of mantra should sit down as he did previously. 9.33cd: He should perform all the previously mentioned placements (nyāsa) fivefold, consisting of the nature of Bhairava.
9.34ab: One should place the God of gods, Navātman, on the northern horn;
9.34cd: Bhairavasadbhāva in the center, and Ratiśekhara on the southern [horn].
9.35ab: He is adorned with a left ear [made] from red skin, flesh, and threads.
9.35cd: One should designate [the mantra] joined with the *bindu* as the *prameyota*, the *ratiśekhara*.
9.36ab: Having performed the *śākta* [rite] as before, the wise one should offer libations as before.
9.36cd: Having worshipped the Lord of Gods once more, he should with devotion address him as follows.
9.37ab: O Supreme Lord, you yourself have recognized me as your guru. 9.37cd: Disciples impelled by the power of Śiva are to be favored by you.
9.38ab: Therefore, these individuals of that same nature have arrived; please bestow your grace upon them.
9.38cd: "Having entered my body, by means of which I shall become equal to you," 9.39ab:
"I shall act in this manner"—thus addressed, [the disciple], his eyes wide with joy, 9.39cd:
should then meditate upon the sixfold path presided over by him.
9.40ab: One should contemplate that the five acts, beginning with creation, are to be accomplished by him.
9.40cd: Through his powers, he possesses the form of the individual soul (jīva); thus his [nature] is twofold: both supreme (parā) and non-supreme (aparā).
9.41ab: By means of the distinction between the formed and the formless, this [power] follows me as well.
9.41cd: Those mantras, beginning with the *hṛdaya*, become the instruments (*karaṇa*) for this [deity].
9.42ab: Having meditated upon Śiva in such a manner, with an inner self absorbed in Him, 9.42cd: one should contemplate oneself as being composed of that [Śiva] and revolve Śiva tenfold.
9.43ab: Having recited all the mantras situated in the womb and the enclosure three times;
9.43cd: Then, having understood the white turban (*sitoṣṇīṣa*) and having empowered it with the ninefold self by reciting [the mantra] seven times;
9.44ab: One should then form the Hand of Śiva (*śivahasta*), which effects the loosening of bonds.

9.44cd: Having washed one's hand with scented water, [one should use] some hand [to apply it]. 9.45ab: Smeared with fragrance, one should worship the God together with his limbs, though without a formal seat.
9.45cd: One should perform the ritual touching (*ālabhana*) within oneself, as well as the grasping (*grahaṇa*) and the joining (*yojana*).
9.46ab: As well as separation, extraction, the cutting of bonds, and so forth; 9.46cd:
having thus attained the state of a Lord through the pervasion of the phenomenal world, 9.47ab:
one should then contemplate oneself as distinct [from Śiva], yet possessing qualities equal to His.
9.47cd: "I myself am present here within the mandala, like a witness over all ritual acts. 9.48ab: "I abide in the fire as the locus for the oblation (homa).
9.48cd: "Until the end of the sacrifice, I remain established in the water-pot (kumbha) for the pacification of obstacles."
9.49ab: And in order to accomplish the loosening of the bonds within the body of the disciple, 9.49cd: I, residing directly within my own body, am the agent of the act of grace;
9.50ab: having reflected upon all this, one should contemplate the path to be purified.

9.50cd: By whichever path the mantra-practitioner intends to perform the initiation for his disciples, 9.51ab: he should contemplate everything therein; thus he shall go to the state free from affliction.
9.51cd: Having become non-different from that [path] therein, he should again reflect as follows:
9.52ab: I alone am the supreme reality; this entire world is in me. 9.52cd: I abide as the presiding controller and the agent of everything.
9.53ab: When a living being has attained equality with that [reality], he is called "liberated."
9.53cd: Having reflected thus, one should once again take recourse in the first [element] to be purified.

9.54ab: Therein, one should contemplate the disciple, the maṇḍala, and the fire as being established as one. 9.54cd: Having projected the path to be purified upon the bodies of the disciples, as previously described.

9.55ab: One should resort to the meditation on one’s own pervasion by means of each respective mantra. 9.55cd: Having first understood the cage of bonds—whether adventitious, innate, or pertaining to Śakti—9.56ab: [One should place them] upon the three locations: the arms, the throat, and the tip of the crest-lock.
Then, with his own mantra, he should invoke the principle (*tattva*) by means of the thread of the three qualities (*triguṇatantu*), worship it, and satisfy it; thereafter,
he should lead [the soul] from the womb of those things to be purified into the pervasive womb (*vyāpinī yoni*).
9.57cd: On the path ending with *māyā*, the wise one [should contemplate] that very *vidyā* in its pure state.
9.58ab: Having performed a libation (*saṃtarpaṇa*) upon it, he should strike the disciple with the *astra-mantra*.
9.58cd: Having touched him again on the heart with the "Hand of Śiva" (*śivahasta*), the learned one [proceeds].
9.59ab: One should perform its grasping by means of not being separated from even a mere ray [of light].

9.59cd: Having gone through the path of the *nāḍī*, one should enclose it within the mantra "haṃ hṛt". 9.60ab: Having then established it within oneself, one should contemplate the impregnation (*garbhādhāna*) in the womb.
9.60cd: The practitioner of mantra, endowed with all embryonic rites, [should perform them] with a mantra of three syllables and half a syllable.
9.61ab: The wise one should effect the birth through the perfection of the capacity for being the enjoyer and the enjoyed.
9.61cd: O Sulocanā, the practitioner of mantra should perform this by means of [the mantra] residing in the right horn.
9.62ab: And with the [mantras] beginning with *iṣetvā*, as well as with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) and others, and also with the *apara* mantra;
9.62cd: the wise one should properly offer fifteen oblations.
9.63ab: Thereafter, the wise ones should perform the severing of the bonds for him with the *apara* mantra.
9.63cd: Then, having addressed the Lord of the World (Bhuvaneśa), or likewise the Lord of the Principles (Tattveśvara); 9.64ab: [lacuna] after that, one should command him as follows:
9.64cd: "O Lord of the World, by the command of Śiva, you must not [obstruct] this practitioner."
9.65ab: An obstruction must be created for the traveler’s path to safety;
9.65cd: then one should perform the upward-throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) with that same [mantra] consisting of slightly more than four syllables.
9.66ab: Due to the application of the *avyāpti* mantra, [this is done] separately for the purification of the path.
9.66cd: Having meditated [on each deity], one should offer three oblations for each one.
9.67ab: Then one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the supreme mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
9.67cd: Having raised up the child, one should cause him to abide within oneself and within his own body.
9.68ab: Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, the wise one should offer three oblations with the *mahāpāśupatāstra* mantra for the sake of purifying [the fire] from its reverse order and so forth. 9.69ab:
Then, having dismissed Vāgīśī, he should [dissolve] the *tattva* within that interval.
9.69cd: One should contemplate the pure [soul] as dissolved within the impure, O Supreme Goddess.

9.70ab: When the purification through the pervasion of the end of time has thus been performed with care, 9.70cd: having severed that noose of the arm, one should offer it into the fire together with clarified butter.
9.71ab: But when the Māyātattva has been purified, as well as the bond at the throat, the wise [teacher], 9.71cd:
for the sake of the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*) which completely purifies the path up to the end of Māyā, 9.72ab:
should employ the Aparā [mantra] in those ritual actions (*kriyā*) for which no specific mantra has been mentioned.
9.72cd: And likewise, from Vidyā up to Sakala, one should worship Parāparā.
9.73ab: One should worship the group of eight beginning with Pibantī above Īśvara;
9.73cd: nor, however, should the wise man worship the group of six limbs above Sakala.

9.74ab: Whatever rite is enjoined by the rules should be performed in the Niṣkala [state] by means of the Supreme [mantra]. 9.74cd: But in the Viśuddha [cakra], at the end of the Sakala [state], the wise one, having cut the top-knot (śikhā), 9.75ab: and having offered clarified butter (ājya) into the fire, should then bathe the disciple in the proper sequence.
9.75cd: Having sipped water and worshipped the Lord of Gods, and having filled the *sruva* ladle with clarified butter;
9.76ab: Having likewise established the disciple within himself, he should recollect the root mantra.
9.76cd: [He should contemplate] Śiva, Śakti, himself, the disciple, the clarified butter, and likewise the fire.
9.77ab: Unifying [the breath], one should proceed slowly to the *dvādaśānta* with undistracted mind;

9.77cd: Having established the *kumbhaka* there, meditating upon the one who is both with and without parts (*sakala-niṣkala*), 9.78ab: One should remain unperturbed for as long as the clarified butter (*ājya*) is not exhausted.
9.78cd: When one is thus united with the supreme reality by the Guru, who is the very form of Śiva;
9.79ab: Having burned away the bonds of *māyā*, he does not again fall into the state of a bound soul (*paśu*).
9.79cd: This is the rule declared for the ritual of initiation (*dīkṣā*) in the earthly realm (*bhuvana*).
9.80ab: Having set aside the rules for the other paths as well as the rule for the yoga of Śiva, 9.80cd: and having abandoned the reverse process, [the path] is twofold on the way of the *tattvas*.
9.81ab: Likewise, it is fourfold on the path of the *varṇas* and on the path of the *padas*.
9.81cd: In the path of Mantra it is eightfold, and in that called Kalā it is likewise twofold; 9.82ab: In Trikaṇḍa, that very same [path] is proclaimed to have twenty qualities.
9.82cd: Thus, the purification of all the paths has been briefly proclaimed.
9.83ab: "Now listen as the ritual duties of the practitioner and the teacher are being described.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, on the initiation of ritual action (*kriyādīkṣā*), in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*;
[now begins] the tenth chapter, on consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

10.1ab: Now, [the teacher] should likewise appoint one who is endowed with the [necessary] characteristics, who is intent on the means of attaining success, 10.1cd: who knows the scriptures, self-controlled, wise, free from greed, honest, and steadfast, 10.2ab: without having first tested him for his capacity as a practitioner.
10.2cd: Having worshipped the Supreme Lord according to the prescribed rite as before, 10.3ab:
on the second [day], one should place a flawless jar made of gold or other precious materials, as previously described;
10.3cd: in every case, it should be situated upon the southern petal of the central lotus.
10.4ab: One should worship the individual mantras of the leaders with flowers and other offerings.
10.4cd: Having gratified him with a thousand [offerings], one should perform the consecration.
10.5ab: Having placed [the deity] upon an auspicious and beautiful throne made of *śrīparṇī* wood.
10.5cd: Facing east or north, bathed, and adorned with flowers and other ornaments; 10.6ab: Having properly formed his body with mantras and having duly performed auspicious rites;
10.6cd: Amidst the sounding of conchs, kettledrums, and the like, and the auspicious chanting of the Vedas.
10.7ab: Having performed his consecration with all royal honors, 10.7cd:
and having meditated upon him as equal to Sadāśiva, one should then adorn him.
10.8ab: Having worshipped the Lord of Gods once more, the wise one should impart the mantra to him.
10.8cd: Accompanied by flowers, unbroken rice grains, and sesame seeds, [and] water, he should place [the vessel] upon his head.
10.9ab: He too, having likewise resorted to that form on the right side of the head, 10.9cd: and having consecrated it with the *astra* mantra, should then manifest the power (*śakti*) of Rudra.
10.10ab: Embraced by her, he should satisfy that mantra with a thousand [offerings]. 10.10cd: From that time forward, being devoted to it, he shall possess qualities equal to hers.
10.11ab: This is the consecration of the teacher, [accompanied] by the ritual of the mantra, excluding the lacuna.
10.11cd: But for him, [the state] accompanied by the words of consecration...

10.12ab: Thus this state is to be attained; it is difficult to attain for those of unrefined self. 10.12cd: For the sake of attaining mantra-perfection, the practitioner should observe the mantra-vow.

10.13ab: Having performed this as prescribed for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one should bathe and recite the mantra of the Lord of Knowledge (*vidyādhipa*). 10.13cd: One should recite it one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*) and perform its libation (*tarpaṇa*) with a tenth part of that number.
10.14ab: Having performed the consecration again as before, one should recite the *Brahmaśiras* mantra.
10.14cd: Having become one with that object of focus (*lakṣya*), being free from lassitude, [one should recite] two hundred thousand [times].
10.15ab: And two hundred thousand for Rudrāṇī, and four hundred thousand for the much-praised Puruṣṭuta. 10.15cd: O Goddess, one should mutter the Mahāpāśupata [mantra] five hundred thousand times.
10.16ab: Clad in variegated garments and ornaments of white, red, yellow, and black;
10.16cd: one who is thus protected by these mantras shall become peerless.
10.17ab: Augmented by the power of the mantra, he is beyond the reach of all malevolent beings.
10.17cd: Having thus observed the vow, whatever [deity] one wishes to accomplish, 10.18ab:
having offered the *argha* to that [deity], one should reverently recite the nine-lakṣa mantra. 10.18cd:
And from the fire-oblation (*homa*) of excellent substances, there should be a libation (*tarpaṇa*) consisting of a tenth part of that.
10.19ab: Those who know [the matter] say that the *mahākṣmāpāla* seeds are the best, and so forth;
10.19cd: Having doubled [the amount] for the middling, and likewise tripling it for the inferior;
10.20ab: Clarified butter, *guggulu*, human fat, and "great meat" are considered equal [in potency].

10.20cd: Curd, bilva, milk, and lotus are proclaimed to be equal to the earth (clay). 10.21ab: The emblic myrobalan, dūrvā grass, amṛtā, and fish are considered to be exactly equal to clarified butter (ājya).
10.21cd: Then, one should perform [the rite] with sesame seeds and the others, in the sequence of nine, six, and threefold [repetitions].
10.22ab: Having first performed this [rite] in this manner, the wise one should offer the *argha* for the sake of success (*siddhi*).
10.22cd: Having offered the *argha*, he should recite [the mantra] until the desired success is attained.
10.23ab: By means of a single hundred thousand [recitations], one becomes a lord of the earth together with his servants, army, and vehicles.
10.23cd: O Goddess, by two [mantras] one brings [others] under control; one shall obtain a kingdom.
10.24ab: By three, there is the attainment of hidden treasures; by four, the success of powers.
10.24cd: By five, the entire earth; by six, the host of apsarases.
10.25ab: With seven [lakṣas] one reaches the seven worlds, and with ten one becomes equal to him (Śiva).
10.25cd: From there, O Maheśvarī, with fifty [lakṣas] one goes to the end of the Unmanifest (avyakta).
10.26ab: One reaches the end of Māyā with sixty lakṣas, and the end of Īśvara with eighty.
10.26cd: For one who has performed ten million recitations, success is achieved over the entire extent of the earth.
10.27ab: Alternatively, having performed the service as prescribed, one should possess the mind of a hero.
10.27cd: On a night during the day of the black Bhūta, one should perform this ritual.
10.28ab: Having performed the sacrifice previously described and having offered the subsequent substances, 10.28cd:
the mantra-practitioner, with body erect and facing north, should recite the mantra while remaining perfectly motionless.
10.29ab: He should continue until the mistresses of yoga (yogeśvarīs) have arrived from all directions.

10.29cd: Having let out a most terrible and extremely dreadful clamor, 10.30ab: they fall to the ground and remain there, encircling the Lord of the Practitioner within. 10.30cd: Having paid homage to them, he pierces his own left side.
10.31ab: Then, by giving the *argha* offering to them with that [substance] produced from it, one becomes equal to them.
10.31cd: And the teacher (*ācārya*) too, observing silence, should perform this daily for six months.
10.32ab: As for the fifteen mantras that were previously spoken by me to you—
10.32cd: Equipped with the previously mentioned ritual placement (*nyāsa*), performing the fire-rite (*vahnikārya*) three times a day;

10.33ab: One should meditate upon the trident described earlier, while remaining established in celibacy (*brahmacarya*). 10.33cd: Having performed the sacrifice (*yāga*) described earlier, which is encircled by the three powers (*triśakti*).
10.34ab: At that time, the instructor should consecrate himself both at the beginning and at the end.
10.34cd: Having thus fulfilled his vow, the mantra-practitioner becomes the most excellent knower of mantras.
10.35ab: Performing the acts of restraint and grace, he is not obstructed.

10.35cd: One should place the three [syllables] of the root-mantra upon the three [parts], beginning with the middle, on the two purified [hands]. 10.36ab: [One places] *vāmā* on the left thumb, *tule* on the eyes, and *astram* on the index finger.
10.36cd: With the fragment *akṣahrīṃ*, one should install the *śabdarāśi*.
10.37ab: By means of this [mantra] *naphahrīm*, the wise one [should worship] the form of Śakti;
10.37cd: and by the practice of the reversed Mahāmudrā, the Root [Mantra] itself.
10.38ab: Likewise, the placement of the limbs (*aṅga*) in their respective locations—this is the general ritual of placement (*nyāsa*).
Thus ends the tenth chapter, the Section on Initiation (*Abhiṣeka*), in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara*.
Now begins the eleventh chapter, the Section on Initiation (*Dīkṣā*):
11.1ab: "Henceforth, I shall fully explain initiation, which is most difficult to obtain."
11.1cd: It perfectly bestows both enjoyment and liberation, and produces immediate conviction.
11.2ab: For this [practice], nothing at all such as a mandala or a kuṇḍa is required.
11.2cd: Nor is there any need for prior ritual placements (nyāsa) and so forth, or bathing and the like; it may be performed according to one's desire.
11.3ab: Having entered the sacrificial hall, which is well-smeared and beautifully adorned, 11.3cd: facing either east or north, and well-decorated with fine flowers and garments, 11.4ab:
having recollected the blazing Śakti from the tips of the feet up to the head...
11.4cd: One should contemplate the body as completely consumed by the practice of Mahāmudrā.

11.5ab: And through the practice of the direct order (*anuloma*), one should contemplate Mālinī, who possesses the radiance of nectar. 11.5cd: With a mind absorbed in that meditation, one should contemplate her for the sake of the perfection of the body.
11.6ab: Then one should contemplate the previously mentioned path to be purified within the body. 11.6cd:
Having thus purified the constituent elements, one should lead them to the state of immortality by means of Śakti alone.
11.7ab: Mālinī, situated in the middle of the supreme encapsulation (parāsaṃpuṭa), [is used] in all ritual acts.
11.7cd: O Dear One, one who knows the ritual procedure should employ either the supreme [mantra] alone;
11.8ab: having first worshipped Gaṇeśa for the pacification of obstacles;
11.8cd: thereafter, beginning with one's own guru, one should worship the lineage of gurus.
11.9ab: Then, beneath Gaṇeśa, one should worship the entire collection of mantras.
11.9cd: Thereafter, one should fully worship the *argha* offering for their lords right there.
11.10ab: Beneath the last [deity], one should worship Vidyā; likewise, one should worship Maheśvarī-Vidyā.
11.10cd: Within the circle of mantra-knowledge and vidyās, one should establish the Kula-śakti.
11.11ab: In the east, south, west, and north, one should place the four beginning with Māheśī.
11.11cd: Likewise, starting from Indrāṇī, they should be placed up to the end of the petals in the northeast and other directions.

11.12ab: There, one should place the deity above with this seed-syllable (bīja) in the form of a peak (kūṭa). 11.12cd: The individual soul (jīva), mounted upon the staff and situated atop the trident, [should be placed].
11.13ab: Then, below that, the right finger; then, the left breast.
11.13cd: Then, below the navel and throat, [he is] adorned by the left shoulder.
11.14ab: Afterwards, he is endowed with the tongue of Śiva, and above that, with the upper lip. 11.14cd: He is declared to be the sovereign of all the circles of Yoginīs.
11.15ab: By the mere utterance of this [mantra] as well, the consciousness taught by others shall arise.

11.15cd: Thereafter, one should worship the group of eight heroes (vīrāṣṭaka) according to the procedure prescribed for Śakti. 11.16ab: Having worshipped with abundant and various perfumes, incenses, garlands, and so forth, [one should proceed].
11.16cd: One should fashion a name preceded by the syllable *Śrī* and ending with the word *pāda*.

11.17ab: Then, having summoned the disciple who has been thoroughly examined in many ways, 11.17cd: and having sprinkled him with the power of Rudra (*rudraśakti*), one should place him before the deity.
11.18ab: Having gazed upon his two arms, one should inflame them with the power of Rudra (rudra-śakti).
11.18cd: In that same manner, one should offer a flower onto the two hands smeared with fragrant unguents.
11.19ab: Having meditated on those two as being without support, one should contemplate them as drawn forth by the Power (śakti).
11.19cd: Having bound his eyes as before with a thread empowered by the *śakti*-mantra, 11.20ab: he should then cause him to cast a flower; that *śakti* resides in his hand. 11.20cd:
One should identify his *kula* according to where that flower falls.
11.21ab: Having opened his mouth, one should afterwards cause him to fall at [the teacher’s] feet.
11.21cd: Then, the knower of yoga, having worshipped the *cakra* on his head and in his two hands, 11.22ab: Should impel those two hands with force until they reach the top of the head.
11.22cd: The ritual of Śiva’s Hand has been proclaimed; it produces immediate conviction.
11.23ab: Thereafter, one should cause the sacrificial pap (caruka) made from fruits such as dates to be given.
11.23cd: Having made the body of the disciple supported by the Power (Śakti), one should place it before [the deity].
11.24ab: Having drawn back the right hand by means of the practice of scattering flowers, 11.24cd:
the mantra-practitioner, with his mind fixed on that visualization, should cause [the disciple] to take the sacrificial oblation (caru).
11.25ab: By means of the application of the Śiva-hand, having placed it [upon the head], he should lead it to the mouth.
11.25cd: By this very procedure, O Goddess, one should offer a tooth-stick produced from a milk-tree, sixteen finger-breadths in length. 11.26ab:
By observing their movements, the mantra-practitioner should examine the descent of power (śaktipāta).
11.27ab: The wise one [should know] those [impurities] as mild, intense, and so forth, according to their respective distinctions of mildness, intensity, and so on.

11.27cd: Thus, this initiate (samayin) is described as abiding by the path already taught. 11.28ab: And when he desires to undergo initiation, having surrendered his mind to Him alone, [he should proceed].

11.28cd: Having worshipped that Lord of the Kula in the same manner as before, the yogin, having honored him in due order as previously described, should look upon the disciple whose body is upright. 11.29cd: The wise one, having meditated on the Śakti extending from the tips of the feet to the top of the head, [should contemplate it].

11.30ab: Then, having projected the path to be purified and the discourse on the pervasion of all paths, 11.30cd: according to the previously mentioned method through the divisions beginning with the *śakti-tattva*, 11.31ab: one should sit down and then perform this ritual procedure for him.

11.31cd: Starting from the root to be purified, one should [visualize] the Śakti, possessing the radiance of blazing fire; 11.32ab: With a mind focused on meditative cultivation, one should unite her with the purification of that which is to be purified.
11.32cd: Thus, she burns away all things to be purified, being free from all affliction.
11.33ab: One should contemplate [the breath] merged within Śiva, whether in the partless (niṣkala) or the with-parts (sakala).
11.33cd: When joined by the yogi upon the path, it nourishes that which is of its own kind. 11.34ab: It consumes everything else—the entire collection of that which is of a different kind.

11.34cd: As this disciple is being purified by her, the one of great intelligence (mahāmati) 11.35ab: Should attentively observe the collection of signs beginning with bliss (ānanda). 11.35cd: Bliss, rising, trembling, sleep, and the fifth, whirling (ghūrṇi).

11.36ab: Thus, by means of the power that has entered [the body], according to its distinctions of mildness, intensity, and so forth, 11.36cd: one should perform the paralyzing of the fetters (pāśastobha) and the seizing of the bound soul (paśugraha) as desired.
11.37ab: For the one who has been seized, one should again perform the assignment (niyoga) for the consumption of the remainder.
11.37cd: Or, if this possession does not arise in anyone at all;
11.38ab: then one should burn him simultaneously with power, both externally and internally. 11.38cd: Being thus consumed by that [power], he becomes like a tree whose roots have been severed.
11.39ab: He falls upon the surface of the earth, or he causes a displacement [of the disciple].
11.39cd: But even if this should happen, one should not abandon such a person, just as one does not discard a stone.
11.40ab: For one who lacks the necessary fitness, initiation is performed according to the rule for a separate reality (*tattva*).
11.40cd: One should perform [the rite] according to the method of practicing the reality (*tattva*) that will be described hereafter.

11.41ab: Thus, for this seeker of liberation who has been initiated, the remaining course of conduct is as follows. 11.41cd: The *kulakrameṣṭi* (family-lineage sacrifice), accompanied by the five states (*pañcāvasthā*), should be prescribed.

11.42ab: But one who desires to enjoy [the fruits of yoga] should properly perform the consecration of yoga (yogābhiṣeka). 11.42cd: Having there worshipped the body as before with extensive and wise deities, 11.43ab: [One should offer] eight lamps made of gold and other materials, with red wicks and ghee.
11.43cd: Having awakened Śiva by means of the eight families (*kulāṣṭaka*), one should worship Him within a conch shell.

11.44ab: [The conch] which contains all kinds of jewels and medicinal herbs, and is filled with scented water. 11.44cd: With that [water], one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) upon Him according to the procedure taught for the Hand of Śiva (*śivahasta*).
11.45ab: This is the consecration of the teacher, endowed with the station of authority.
11.45cd: One should likewise offer sixty-four lamps along with the *piṇḍas* and other offerings.
11.46ab: Indeed, in the very rite of consecration, [it is performed] by the entire assembly of yogins.
11.46cd: Once these two have been recognized there, the Guru shall become the bestower of liberation.
11.47ab: To these two, he should fully impart all three kinds of knowledge.
11.47cd: The Yogin should then give his own command regarding the performance of their respective duties.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the Section on Initiation, in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*.
The twelfth chapter, the Section on Concentration (Dhāraṇā), begins:
12.1ab: Then, having heard these very clear words of the God of Gods...
12.1cd: With eyes blossoming with great joy, she who brings delight to the world; 12.2ab: Satiated by the nectar of contentment, the goddess worshipped by the hosts of gods;
12.2cd: Having bowed to the slayer of Andhaka, she spoke these words once again.
12.3ab: You previously stated that a yogi should practice yoga;
12.3cd: O Destroyer of Tripura, tell me how that practice is to be performed.
12.4ab: Thus addressed by the Mother of the World, Bhairava, the destroyer of fear, [spoke].
12.4cd: The noble-minded one spoke these words, clear and profound:
12.5ab: "O Goddess, listen as I describe the method for the practice of yoga, 12.5cd: by means of which, once it has become firm, a yogi shall attain perfection in this world."

12.6ab: In a cave, or even in an underground chamber, that is silent and very delightful, 12.6cd: and entirely free from all disturbances, the yogi should practice yoga. 12.7ab: Having mastered his posture, mastered his mind, mastered his breath, and mastered his senses.
12.7cd: Having conquered sleep, conquered anger, and conquered agitation, and being free from distress;
12.8ab: either by piercing the targets or else through the differentiation of the mind;
12.8cd: the Lord of Yogins shall accomplish everything, from the earth up to the power of Śakti.
12.9ab: Through the distinctions of space, form, point, phoneme, world, and sound, 12.9cd:

the sixfold division of the object of focus (lakṣya) is traditionally taught; it is now explained correctly. 12.10ab: By means of the distinction between external and internal, and by their combination.
12.10cd: Space is proclaimed to be threefold; the *bindu* is held to be tenfold.
12.11ab: Shaped like a *kadamba* flower bud, it has the radiance of a shimmering star.
12.11cd: Although it is one, it is considered tenfold through the distinctions of white and other colors.
12.12ab: Sound is tenfold, through its divisions such as Ciñciṇī, Cīravāka, and so forth;
12.12cd: And the body, though divided into two by the distinction of one's own atoms, is manifold.
12.13ab: There is no fixed number of worlds, but that of the phonemes is fifty.
12.13cd: Even when there is but a single goal to be accomplished, one may perceive [other results] here by way of association;
12.14ab: other fruits may also arise, and that is called a difference of the object perceived (lakṣya-bheda).
12.14cd: Where there is only a single fruit, yet a distinction of mental states occurs, that is considered [a case of] mental differentiation (citta-bheda).
12.15ab: One whose self is purified by the initiation of the fire-oblation (homa-dīkṣā) and who possesses the instruction on immersion (samāveśa), 12.15cd:
should first practice that yoga which he desires to accomplish. 12.16ab: Having placed the supreme seed-syllable (parā-bīja) upon the two hands, one should contemplate the Power (śakti).

12.16cd: By means of the application of Mahāmudrā in this inverted procedure, the wise one [should act]. 12.17ab: [Visualizing her] resembling a blazing fire from the tips of her feet to the top of her head, 12.17cd: he should then perform a prostration while holding his breath in the heart.
12.18ab: One should contemplate the seed-syllable of the Supreme (Parā) in its own form as intensely radiant.
12.18cd: One should meditate on its three measures (mātrās) as they emerge from the three cavities (kha). 12.19ab: Then, after a hundred claps (tālas), the yogi shall attain immersion (samāveśa).
12.19cd: For even a slayer of a Brahmin, if he should practice [this] every day for seven days;
12.20ab: One whose body has been thus possessed should perform the prescribed rite.
12.20cd: Furthermore, he who has already had the sequence of the rite of possession performed by his teacher at the outset.
12.21ab: By the power of his latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he should begin the conquest of the stages (*bhūmikā*).
12.21cd: Having paid homage to the Lord of the Gaṇas and having recollected the lineage of the three Gurus, 12.22ab:
he should meditate with undistracted mind so that his body may become perfectly possessed [by the deity].
12.22cd: One's own body becomes like gold, four-cornered, and marked with the thunderbolt.
12.23ab: Thereafter, it attains heaviness within twenty-seven days.
12.23cd: After the seventh day, a state of numbness arises in it.
12.24ab: Within six months, having conquered disease, one becomes like molten gold; 12.24cd: And within three years, possessing a body of diamond, one attains the prowess of nine elephants.
12.25ab: This pure meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*) pertaining to the earth has thus been described to you.
12.25cd: O Goddess, in the first division consisting of fifteen parts as previously described, 12.26ab:
one should visualize the body as active, with a radiance like molten gold, 12.26cd:
seated within a square mandala adorned with vajras.
12.27ab: Within seven days he attains heaviness; within a month, he is freed from disease.
12.27cd: Within six months, while remaining within the earth, he knows everything in its true nature.
12.28ab: Within three years, he enjoys the earth, which has the seven oceans as its girdle.
12.28cd: The second variety has been described; now hear the third.
12.29ab: One should likewise contemplate the body, but as being devoid of activity.
12.29cd: One obtains the previously mentioned fruit, as well as that associated with Pātāla.
In the fourth [state], one should meditatively contemplate [the deity] situated in the heart, twelve finger-breadths in length,
possessing its original color and form, and actively engaged in its function, without weariness.
Having attained all that was previously described, one becomes the lord of Pātāla.
12.31cd: One attains that very same stability when the fifth [breath] is indeed motionless.
12.32ab: In the sixth, one should meditate on [the light] as yellow, resembling a shimmering sun, yet shrouded by dark clouds.
12.32cd: Likewise, the wise practitioner should remember it as waveless even in the seventh.
12.33ab: When both of these have become firm, he knows and enjoys the three worlds—Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar—in exactly the same number of years previously mentioned. 12.34ab:
He perceives his own self, golden-hued, situated within the heart, in its entirety.

12.34cd: One should contemplate [the self] as having its entire body illuminated by its own radiance. 12.35ab: One should likewise contemplate the seven worlds according to their distinctions of activity and so forth, as before.
12.35cd: When this ninth distinction has become firm, the wise one knows and enjoys [them].
12.36ab: One should visualize the two [forms] as yellow, resembling the orb of the sun, as before.
12.36cd: One attains the world of Brahmā by the very path previously described.
12.37ab: The great [form], twice-aspected and yellow, shines below as before.
12.37cd: Having become equal to me, one should meditate; such a person goes to my world.

12.38ab: One should meditate on the all-illuminating light, yellow in color, pervading both the internal and the external. 12.38cd: By so meditating, one shall attain the sovereignty over the hundred Rudras.
12.39ab: Thus, having practiced the earth-element in fifteen ways, 12.39cd:
by yogis for the sake of attaining yoga, out of a desire for its fruits; 12.40ab: whichever latent impression (vāsanā) one possesses, that alone becomes subject to one's capacity.

12.40cd: At the time of initiation, the wise should employ him right there [in that specific principle]. 12.41ab: Whosoever is joined to whichever reality-level (tattva), from that he does not turn back.
12.41cd: Having attained all the fruit thereof, being united with Śiva, he attains liberation.

12.42ab: Even one who is unyoked, having attained purification of the paths from the Lord of the World, 12.42cd: being pure and with the bonds of transmigratory existence burnt away, attains the state of Śiva.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, the Section on the First Concentration (*dhāraṇā*), in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*.
The thirteenth chapter, concerning the mastery of the great elements such as water, is completed.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain this Vāruṇī dhāraṇā.
13.1cd: By means of which, through perfected yoga, one becomes a lord over the depths of the waters;
13.2ab: The yogi should visualize his body situated within the water—white, cool, and perfectly round;
13.2cd: [Visualizing it] both internally and externally, he should reflect that nothing else exists.

13.3ab: For one who practices in this manner, a state of moistening occurs within seven days. 13.3cd: He certainly becomes free from bile-related diseases within a month. 13.4ab: His limbs become supple, his vision becomes clear, and his hair becomes dark and curly.
13.4cd: Within a year, the lord of yogins becomes one who rains like a cloud.
13.5ab: Thus has been described this first pure concentration (dhāraṇā), known as Vāruṇī. 13.5cd: Now I shall further explain this [concentration] as divided by its various distinctions.
13.6ab: One should contemplate one’s own body as before, white and engaged in activity; 13.6cd: situated upon water, O Goddess, with the inner self absorbed therein.
13.7ab: Within seven days, one is liberated from all diseases arising from bile (pitta).

13.7cd: Stability arises after six months, provided one has attained absorption in that [state]. 13.8ab: Through three years, the realization of the water-envelopement occurs for him. 13.8cd: Even when there is no differentiation of activity, he is everywhere like Varuṇa.
13.9ab: He goes to the principle of Varuṇa; one should practice the stages (bhūmikās) in succession.
13.9cd: As before, one should contemplate the Self situated in the middle of the throat, twelve finger-breadths [above it].
13.10ab: By recollecting the Lord of the water-principle, one certainly beholds Him before long.
13.10cd: When the fifth [element] is stable, that vision attains stability in its own nature. 13.11ab:
Even when the lunar disc, though double-folded and densely veiled, has become stabilized, 13.11cd:
it then attains equality with that [vision], and thus [the goddess] assumes her complete form.
13.12ab: One should contemplate the body being filled with white-colored radiance;
13.12cd: that very [body] attains stability once [the radiance] has become perfectly steady. 13.13ab:
Thereafter, one should contemplate it as having the luster of the moon's orb released from the clouds.
13.13cd: He attains the state of its lord; in the second [state], he reaches stability.
13.14ab: Then one should contemplate the white light that shines downwards.
13.14cd: One attains the status of a Vidyeśvara, arising from the veil of water.
13.15ab: When white light, pervading one’s own body, is meditated upon as being situated there, 13.15cd:

one attains sovereignty over all, provided it remains firmly established there. 13.16ab: When [the mind] is firm in the three states, there is equality with the reality that is the object of meditation.
13.16cd: And when there is a pair, O Lord, consciousness arises [of that state].
13.17ab: When there is another pair, the knower of yoga becomes stable, equal to that [state].
13.17cd: In the group of six, he attains sovereignty over all; but in the other pair, there is a fall.

13.18ab: Thus, this procedure within the fifteenfold division among all the principles (tattvas) should be known by those who understand the ritual methods as bestowing the accomplishment of the five fruits. 13.18cd–13.19ab:
Any other fruit different from this that has been mentioned or will yet be spoken of [is also included].
13.19cd: All that should be known as the secondary fruit resulting from non-investigation.
13.20ab: Thus, this Vāruṇī has been described with its fifteen divisions.
13.20cd: Now hear about the Āgneyī for the sake of the yogis' accomplishment of yoga.
13.21ab: One should contemplate the body as a triangle, enveloped by rows of red flames.
13.21cd: The fire arising from one's own body blazes forth, indeed burning everything.
13.22ab: O Goddess, within seven days, its intensity is produced.
13.22cd: Through all [the disorders] arising from wind and phlegm, the practitioner is freed from them within a month.
13.23ab: He becomes devoid of sleep, eats much, and produces very little feces and urine.
13.23cd: Due to the cessation of the seasonal flow, he may burn away by his will whatever object he touches.
13.24ab: Having become like fire after three years, he plays with fire as he desires;
13.24cd: when enraged, he utterly consumes everything, including the mountains, forests, and groves.
13.25ab: One should contemplate oneself as mounted upon a triangular mandala.
13.25cd: The wise one, through the distinction of activity and so forth, [perceives] everywhere;
13.26ab: Freed from diseases within seven days, he becomes like fire within six months; 13.26cd: In three years, he beholds the complete principle of radiant energy (*tejastattva*).
13.27ab: Whatever is observed when there is a distinction in power remains stable when that [power] is distinguished.

13.27cd: As before, meditating upon oneself as being situated in the middle of the palate and possessing the radiance of fire, 13.28ab: one perceives, in succession, all the lords of the principles (*tattva*) of light.
13.28cd: Resembling a fire enveloped in smoke and having a form like the orb of the sun;
13.29ab: Meditating upon that splendor within [the heart], one attains equality with the Lord of the Tattvas.
13.29cd: It is the light that destroys the web of darkness, possessing a radiance like a smokeless fire.

13.30ab: Meditating upon the entire [deity] right there, one attains the state of its lord. 13.30cd: One should contemplate the splendor there as having the brilliance of the sun and fire. 13.31ab: Having attained firm stability therein, one reaches the status of a Lord of Mantras.
13.31cd: Therein he should manifest a splendor resembling a gem-lamp.
13.32ab: Having attained identity with that, the yogi reaches the state of being the Lord of the Lords of Mantras.
13.32cd: Meditating on the light both internal and external, he becomes absorbed in it everywhere.
13.33ab: Therefore, he does not fall from that state until the time of reabsorption, remaining unbroken.
13.33cd: But at the time of reabsorption, he attains the supreme, peaceful state of Śaṅkara.
13.34ab: Thus, this fifteenfold concentration on fire (vahnidhāraṇā) has been described.
13.34cd: One should contemplate one’s own body as black, circular, and marked with six dots;
13.35ab: It is mobile and accompanied by the sound "sacūcū," for one has resorted to the wind-element concentration (*vāyavī dhāraṇā*).
13.35cd: This mobility arises from the severing of diseases born of phlegm (*kapha*), becoming like the wind itself.
13.36ab: For six months the yogin should practice with his inner self absorbed in that;
13.36cd: having traveled a hundred *yojanas*, he returns in a mere moment without fatigue.
13.37ab: But in three years, he becomes one who visibly assumes the form of the wind.
13.37cd: It pulverizes masses of mountains and even uproots trees;
13.38ab: When enraged, it shakes Śakra along with his servants, forces, and vehicles.
13.38cd: One should contemplate one’s own body as resembling black collyrium.
13.39ab: One attains everything previously mentioned within six months; there is no doubt in this matter.
13.39cd: After three years, having attained identity with it, one perceives the reality of Vāyu.
13.40ab: One should meditate on the form of the Self between the eyebrows as resembling collyrium.
13.40cd: He perceives all the swift-moving lords of the wind-element (vāyutattva) as well;
13.41ab: Having a form like the radiant orb of a sapphire covered by clouds, 13.41cd: Meditating upon it, he attains equality with it when he becomes completely absorbed in it.
13.42ab: One should meditate there upon the entire [body] as resembling a split sapphire.
13.42cd: Thereby one attains the state of a Lord of Mantras, and subsequently even lordship over that.
13.43ab: When that color is meditated upon as pervading all, one shall attain splendor.
13.43cd: Then one attains invincibility; therein, [the breath] flows upwards and downwards.
13.44ab: Thus has been described this divine concentration (*dhāraṇā*) arising from the vital air (*vāyu*).
13.44cd: Having meditated upon one's own body as being like the wind, and recollecting its absence [therein].
13.45ab: In seven days, the yogi attains emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
13.45cd: Within a single month, even if bitten by the lords of serpents (*bhogīndra*), he does not lose consciousness.
13.46ab: He is freed from all diseases and becomes devoid of wrinkles and grey hair.

13.46cd: Within six months, he will take on the form of the sky and pass even through minute apertures. 13.47ab: After three years, he will become manifest as the sky itself. 13.47cd: By his mere will he may assume a massive body, and likewise by his will a subtle body.

13.48ab: Being both uncuttable and unbreakable, he perceives the earth as full of holes; 13.48cd: [He perceives] his own body as being like a pit of saline soil, with the remains of the sap of the *śatapushpa* flower. 13.49ab: For one who contemplates the body in this way for three years, the knowledge of the sky (*vyoma-jñāna*) arises.
13.49cd: And one shall obtain all the previously mentioned fruits within seven days and so forth.
13.50ab: Likewise, one should contemplate [the deity] on the forehead, extending twelve finger-breadths in length.
13.50cd: One beholds all the respective lords of the principles (tattvas) standing before oneself in their proper order.
13.51ab: Meditating on [the deity] as resembling the lunar orb eclipsed by Rāhu, one attains equality with him.
13.51cd: One should contemplate [the deity] as possessing all parts (sakala), resembling the lunar orb, and situated therein.
13.52ab: One attains the status of a Lord of Mantras (mantreśa) through that, and through the moonlight, even the state of Indra.

By that very [power] flowing downwards, the wise one, having attained the state of a Lord of the Lords of Mantras (mantreśvareśatā) both externally and internally, shall obtain incomparable gnosis (vijñāna). And by that [power] flowing upwards, which is of the nature of nectar like moonlight—
13.54ab: Having attained independence, one is not obstructed anywhere.
13.54cd: Thus, the meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) on the five principles have been proclaimed.
13.55ab: But consciousness residing in the pure [principles] and so forth is the possession by the elements (*bhūtāveśa*), which here is fivefold.
13.55cd: Fixing the mind upon those very [objects], there is for oneself the destruction of weariness and other [defilements].
13.56ab: Even in another perception, whatever it may be, according to one's own desire;
13.56cd: one should properly steady the mind; through that, one enjoys its fruit.

13.57ab: Even this single [practice], when cultivated, leads to the state of being an obstacle due to its internal subdivisions. 13.57cd: It becomes an impediment; therefore, one should not establish a fixed attachment there.
13.58ab: Those who establish a fixed attachment there will not attain the supreme fruit.

13.58cd: When the fivefold *dhāraṇā* is mastered, the eight qualities beginning with the state of a *piśāca* [are attained]. 13.59ab: Or else, for yogins, the five [states] ending with that of Indra are accomplished according to their specific distinctions.
13.59cd: The fifteen desired stages are to be cultivated in their proper sequence.
13.60ab: One should accomplish the first [type] in three years, the next in two, and another in one;
13.60cd: Another in six months, and yet another in five, four, or indeed three [months];
13.61ab: [Another] in two [months], one [month], a fortnight, ten days, or five days.
13.61cd: For one whose desire is for the separate [attainments], the sequence is as before—by three, by two, or by one.
13.62ab: Having enjoyed the perfection as desired, he attains the eternal state.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, the Section on the Conquest of the Elements, in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*.

The fourteenth chapter: The Section on the Concentrations on the Subtle Elements (Tanmātra). 14.1ab: Now, I shall duly explain the concentrations on the subtle elements, beginning with smell, in their proper order, for the sake of attaining their respective fruits.

14.2ab: One should meditate on the yellow [element], the subtle essence of smell, which is square and measured by the joints, located at the tip of the nostril, and marked with the insignia of a vajra. 14.3ab:
After the tenth day, for the yogin whose mind is focused on nothing else...
14.3cd: Somewhere a fragrance arises, appearing as two-fold and yet manifold.
14.4ab: Then, by means of the mere seasonal cycle, his pure fragrance shall become stable.
14.4cd: Within six months, he will himself become composed entirely of fragrance.

14.5ab: Whatever fragrance pleases one in a particular place, one should apply that [fragrance] there intensely. 14.5cd: Within three years, one attains the desired accomplishment (*siddhi*) pertaining to the five elements (*pāñcabhautika*).
14.6ab: If, after that, one should contemplate the form of the Self (*ātman*) therein...
14.6cd: Within three years, one shall attain the consciousness that perceives the obstruction of odors.
14.7ab: Therein, it is endowed with slight radiance and is devoid of that [physical] maṇḍala.
14.7cd: Meditating thus, one clearly beholds all those who dwell within the obstruction of odors.
14.8ab: Contemplating in this way the reflection that has the appearance described for the earth-principle (*dharātattva*), 14.8cd:
one attains identity with it, as before, when the two [principles] are stabilized.
14.9ab: Having contemplated one's own nature there, as it shines forth while situated below,
14.9cd: He attains lordship over that [element] by the very path previously described.
14.10ab: Recalling everything above this according to what was said regarding the earth-principle (dharātattva), 14.10cd:
he obtains its corresponding fruit, which resides within the veil of fragrance (gandhāvaraṇa).
14.11ab: Therefore, I shall describe the concentration on the form of taste (rasa), which is practiced by yogis;
14.11cd: by means of which the attainment of all tastes occurs for the yogi.
14.12ab: Resembling a water bubble, O King, it is situated at the tip of the channel (nāḍī).

14.12cd: One should contemplate the subtle element of taste (*rasatanmātra*) as being supported at the tip of one's own tongue. 14.13ab: [One should contemplate it] as perfectly cool, possessing the six tastes, and unctuous, with the inner self absorbed therein.
14.13cd: Then, within just a month, the savoring of taste begins for him.
14.14ab: When, having abandoned salt and other [flavors], one has attained sweetness;
14.14cd: then by swallowing that, the yogi shall become a conqueror of death within six months.
14.15ab: Freed from old age and disease, with black hair and the luster of Acyuta.
14.15cd: Practicing this here and there, one may live as long as the moon, stars, and sun. 14.16ab:
Constantly contemplating the true nature of the self in the form of the previously mentioned bubble, 14.16cd:
one attains unobstructed consciousness; what wonder is there in this?

14.17ab: Meditating upon that very [light] endowed with radiance and devoid of support, 14.17cd: after years, he perceives everything resting within the enclosure of *rasa*. 14.18ab: Contemplating above that the reflection and so forth mentioned in the section on the water-element (*jala-tattva*),
14.18cd: One clearly attains everything previously mentioned arising from the enclosure of taste (rasa).

14.19ab: Therefore, I shall describe the auspicious *dhāraṇā* called Rūpavatī, which bestows divine vision. 14.19cd: It is based upon the subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*) for the sake of all accomplishments.

14.20ab: When the yogi, staying in solitude with eyes closed, 14.20cd: beholds that certain something resembling an autumnal twilight cloud; 14.21ab: having fixed the mind there, he remains for ten days.
14.21cd: At that time, he perceives there even the most subtle drops (bindus).
14.22ab: Some among them are white, red, yellow, and others blue.
14.22cd: Having seen them, he should fix his mind upon them with one-pointed attention.
Within six months, one perceives very many forms within them; after three years, those very same forms appear blazing with splendor and stable.
By practicing upon those, after two years, one sees them in the form of actual images.
14.24cd: Then, after one year, he beholds light; after six months, [light] in the form of a person.
14.25ab: After three months, pervasive light; after one month, it has spread everywhere.
14.25cd: And through the sequence of time, he relies upon the previously mentioned covering of forms.
14.26ab: One obtains every fruit and divine vision arises;
14.26cd: Thus, this [state] is free from conceptual construction, brought forth by the practice of *dhāraṇā*.
14.27ab: Here, the fifteenfold division arises spontaneously of its own accord.
14.27cd: Therefore, one should form a firm resolve regarding this; what is the use of other ostentatious treatises?
14.28ab: Hence, I shall now describe to you another [practice] involving touch, 14.28cd: namely, *dhāraṇā*, by means of which the yogi becomes possessed of a vajra-body.
14.29ab: One should contemplate oneself situated within a hexagonal maṇḍala, 14.29cd:
parched, resembling collyrium, and with every limb throbbing and agitated.
14.30ab: Then, O Goddess, within ten days, [it appears] everywhere upon his skin.
14.30cd: Then, by contemplating that [state], there would be a sensation like that of an ant's touch;
14.31ab: having attained a body of vajra, one obtains what was previously described, just as before;
14.31cd: while contemplating the previously mentioned form in the shape of the previously described maṇḍala.
14.32ab: By what can the knowledge that obstructs the reality-principle of touch be prevented?
14.32cd: One should meditate upon oneself as having a diminished mandala for the sake of attaining mastery over that [principle].
14.33ab: Through which perfect accomplishment will one become a knower of all touches?
14.33cd: Having diligently closed his ears and closed his eyes, 14.34ab:
he hears a great sound; he should fix his mind thereon. 14.34cd:
The digestive fire blazes up, and from that, after ten days, [his body is consumed].
14.35ab: Within six months, the cognition of hearing from a distance arises. 14.35cd: At its conclusion, a faint sound is perceived here and there.
14.36ab: That should be known as the "all-pervading self" (sakalātman), attained through its practice with an undistracted mind.
14.36cd: The consciousness that perceives sound, having attained stability, reaches [the state of] *śabdāvaraṇavijñāna*.
14.37ab: Furthermore, the sound that is heard at its conclusion is like the blast of a conch shell.
14.37cd: That form of *pralayākala* should be practiced by those who desire its fruit.
14.38ab: When that very [state] completely obscures other sounds, 14.38cd: it is called "the one devoid of mental constructs" (vijñānākala) in the Aparājita [world]. 14.39ab:
That other [state] which brings delight to the mind is perceived at its conclusion.
14.39cd: That should be known as the *mantra* by yogins who desire yoga.
14.40ab: But that other sound which is heard thereafter, like the resonance of a peaceful bell, 14.40cd: is declared to be the *mantreśa*, the bestower of the fruit of all accomplishments.
14.41ab: At the moment the sound of the bell ceases, whatever sound arises— 14.41cd: That is indeed the station of the Lord of Mantras; it is the great cause of all supernatural powers (*siddhis*).
14.42ab: Just as a lute struck by the wind emits a sound...
14.42cd: One should know that such a resonance (*dhvani*) therein is the state of Śambhu (*śāmbhava-pada*).
14.43ab: Whether separately or in succession, one should practice all of these.
14.43cd: The omniscient one attains the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) that reside within the veil of sound (*śabdāvaraṇa*).
14.44ab: Thus these five meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) upon the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) have been described.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the section on the meditative concentrations upon the subtle elements, in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*.

The Fifteenth Chapter: On the Concentration on the Senses (Akṣadhāraṇādhikāra). 15.1ab: Now, I shall briefly explain, in due order, the eleven concentrations (dhāraṇās) pertaining to the organs beginning with speech and ending with the mind. 15.1cd: I shall fully describe these ten and one [concentrations] in summary.
15.2ab: The wise person should contemplate the word *namaḥ* within his own mouth. 15.2cd: O Madhusūdanī, through silence he attains mastery over speech.
15.3ab: Speech that is unimpeded in all respects proceeds forth after six months.

15.3cd: Within one year, mastery of the meaning of all treatises arises. 15.4ab: His speech itself proceeds adorned with poetic ornaments (*kāvyālaṅkāra*). 15.4cd: After three years, he becomes an author of treatises himself.
15.5ab: Right there, one should contemplate one’s own body in its proper form; 15.5cd: once again, that very same [body] as white, slightly illuminated by a radiance.
15.6ab: One should recollect it from the lunar orb within the essence (rasa) up to the limit of light.
15.6cd: He gradually attains every fruit arising from the restraint of speech. 15.7ab: Having concentrated his mind upon his hand, after six months he perceives an object situated at a distance.
15.7cd: Without doubt, after three years, he grasps an object even across the ocean.

15.8ab: There, first contemplating one's own body as having the luster of a lotus, 15.8cd: one should with devotion [meditate on] the fourteen [forms] through the distinctions of their activities and so forth, 15.9ab:
according to the previously stated rule of time and by the very path described before.

15.9cd: One obtains every fruit that depends upon the *hastāvṛti* [mudrā]. 15.10ab: Meditating with devotion for three years upon his feet in this same manner, 15.10cd: he wanders tirelessly over the earth as far as the ocean's edge in a mere moment.

15.11ab: Having fully worshipped the fourteen [principles] and practicing upon one's own body and so forth, 15.11cd: one obtains all the results as before, established in the fourfold repetition. 15.12ab: Even by steadying the principle of the mind within the anus, one shall attain [the goal].
15.12cd: Within a month, one attains liberation from the disease of existence without delay;
15.13ab: One attains the state of being "of meritorious fame" within three years, even without great effort.
15.13cd: And herein, one shall obtain the fourteenfold fruit as previously described.

15.14ab: With his senses subdued, one should meditate on the *liṅga* according to its essential nature for the duration of one month; 15.14cd: after six months, without effort, one shall attain the power to assume any form at will. 15.15ab: When that fourteen-fold division has been practiced therein, the one of great intelligence—
15.15cd: One obtains all the fruits arising from the enclosure of the *liṅga* as previously described.
15.16ab: For ten days, one should meditate on one's own tongue as having the luster of the moon.
15.16cd: The yogi attains an experience as if the very nature of his own self were that of the tongue.
15.17ab: With a one-pointed mind, he tastes that which is situated at a distance after six months; 15.17cd: But after three years, he directly licks that supreme nectar.
15.18ab: By means of this, the yogi becomes free from old age and death.
15.18cd: Even if one is inclined toward drinking forbidden liquids and the like, one is not overcome by sins.
15.19ab: Contemplating everything else, as well as one’s own body and so forth, just as before;
15.19cd: one undoubtedly obtains the fruit arising from the covering of the tongue.
15.20ab: For one who gradually contemplates his own nose as having the luster of gold, 15.20cd: within ten days, there shall arise the experience of the emptiness of the nose.
15.21ab: After six months, one smells the fragrance even of an object situated at a distance.
15.21cd: Having smelled the scent of one toward whom he has become angry, he shall cause that person to be slain.
15.22ab: But after three years, having attained the divine scent, the knower of yoga, 15.22cd: endowed with freedom from old age, death, and all defects, becomes worthy of divinity.
15.23ab: One should contemplate everything else exactly as it has been described;
15.23cd: one attains the gradual fruit while established in the obstruction of the sense of smell.
15.24ab: Contemplating one's own two eyes as resembling the rising sun...
15.24cd: After ten days, he will experience a discharge of blood from the eyes. 15.25ab: And a great pain arises for him in the forehead.
15.25cd: One should not be afraid, O Great Goddess, nor should one abandon the practice.
15.26ab: By abandoning [the world], he attains blindness; therefore, one should practice with diligent effort. 15.26cd: Within six months, the great yogin becomes possessed of divine vision.
15.27ab: Diligent, he perceives the earth as having openings, reaching to the edge of the cosmic shell (kaṭāha).

15.27cd: Then, the wise one perceives everything from the impermanent up to the upper limit, as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand. 15.28ab: Within three years, the yogi beholds the very end of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
15.28cd: Within that, the knowledge of the Yoginīs residing within the body arises.
15.29ab: Recalling one's own body and so forth, as well as other things previously mentioned, in the same manner as before;
15.29cd: that one attains everything arising from the removal of the eye-cataract—what is wonderful in this?
15.30ab: Everywhere, recollecting the skin as being like the leaf of the *añjana* plant, free from all waves [of impurity].
15.30cd: Even with weapons, he will not be able to be cut within a month.
15.31ab: After six months, even by an extremely intense fire, he is not burned. 15.31cd: After three years, the yogi [is unharmed] by diamonds, stones, poisons, or serpents.
15.32ab: It is never afflicted; it has attained a state free from old age and death.
15.32cd: Like the [verses on] touch, obstruction, impulse, and cognition, there are fourteen [categories].
15.33ab: These varieties, along with their fruits, are to be understood according to their respective preceding times.
