15.33cd: But in this case, one should contemplate the body as enveloped by one's own body and others;
15.34ab: the wise person, fixing his own mind upon the space of the ear, 15.34cd:
attains the power of hearing from a distance within six months.
15.35ab: O Goddess, within three years, that which is proclaimed within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), 15.35cd: he hears it all clearly, being free from old age and death.
15.36ab: There, one should contemplate everything, beginning with one's own body, as being like empty space.
15.36cd: One obtains every fruit arising from the obstruction of the ear, as previously described.

15.37ab: Therefore, I shall describe the *dhāraṇā* called Manovatī, which bestows all perfections (*siddhi*). 15.37cd: O Goddess, by means of this perfected practice, one may obtain the fruit of all perfections.
15.38ab: The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings. 15.38cd: Therefore, the practitioner should discipline that mind if he desires imperishable liberation.
15.39ab: It resembles a half-moon, facing downward, and is situated in the heart.
15.39cd: By reflecting for just one month, he will attain intuitive insight (*pratibhā*).
15.40ab: Suddenly he sees something, and likewise suddenly he hears something.
15.40cd: Knowledge consisting of all the sense faculties arises suddenly here and there.
15.41ab: Within three years, one who is engaged in yoga will clearly perceive the individual consciousnesses of each respective sense organ.
15.41cd: This becomes perfectly clear for the yogin who is disciplined in yoga.
15.42ab: In this state, one should also recollect one’s own body and so forth, as previously described.
15.42cd: Having attained the consciousness that is the veil of the mind, one obtains the quality of Soma.
15.43ab: Thus, these eleven songs should be practiced by you accordingly. 15.43cd: For the senses are the means, and all fruit is established within them.
15.44ab: The wise have declared that both bondage and liberation depend upon the senses;
15.44cd: when they are restrained, they lead to bondage; when they are released, they lead to liberation.
15.45ab: When these [senses], together with the mind, abide in a pervasive state...
15.45cd: O beloved, they should be known as "liberated" by the wise at that time.
15.46ab: But when they are situated in some other region within the objective field, 15.46cd: then they are declared to be "bound."
15.47ab: Thus, this twofold state, distinguished as pure and impure, has been fully explained regarding the senses in the *Siddhayogīśvarīmata*. 15.47cd:
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, on the Concentration on the Senses (*akṣadhāraṇā*), in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*.
The sixteenth chapter on *dhāraṇā* is completed. 16.1ab: Now, [he describes] the divine *dhāraṇā* consisting of pride, the most excellent of all *dhāraṇās*.
16.1cd: O you who are praised by yogis for your yoga, I shall describe that which produces great pride.
16.2ab: With undistracted mind, one should meditate on the sixteen-spoked wheel as one's own body. 16.2cd: Having reflected, "I am this," [one should visualize it] surrounded by its own retinue.
16.3ab: Within three years, the yogin shall become invincible.
16.3cd: His sense of "mine-ness" (mamatva) shall become undecaying (acyuta) everywhere and in whatever place.
16.4ab: Meditating upon his own form as the nave of such a wheel.
16.4cd: "I am indeed everything; everything is established within me. 16.5ab: "Thereafter, one attains the consciousness of the I-sense (ahaṅkāra)—what wonder is there in this?
16.5cd: "Meditating with unwearied mind upon my own nature within the heart-cakra,"
16.6ab: Without delay, he obtains the fruit born from the veil of pride.
16.6cd: Contemplating Bimba and all the rest in sequence as Nīlalohita, 16.7ab: he attains everything arising from that [state], impelled by the ten stages.
16.7cd: Thus has been described that [meditation] consisting of pride, which bestows the qualities of Prajāpati.
16.8ab: Visualizing within the heart a lotus resembling the orb of the rising sun, 16.8cd:
endowed with the states of dharma and so forth, having eight petals and a pericarp.

16.9ab: Within one month he becomes firm in intellect; within six months he becomes a possessor of the power of retention (*śrutidhara*). 16.9cd: Within three years, he himself becomes a creator of the scriptures. 16.10ab: There, he should contemplate his own form; he beholds the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*).
16.10cd: By meditating upon Brahmā, one attains knowledge of that Lord.
16.11ab: Whether asleep or established in samādhi, the sage utters the Vedas. 16.11cd: Through constant practice, they become clearly manifest even if never formally studied.
16.12ab: Contemplating in sequence all that was previously described, beginning with the *bimba*;
16.12cd: one attains the sovereignty of Brahmā, which rests upon the veil of the intellect (*buddhyāvaraṇa*).
16.13ab: One should meditate on the orb of the sun within the heart, and inside that, the lunar disc.
16.13cd: For one who practices in this way, [the divine eye] arises after six months;
16.14ab: the divine eye [arises] without effort, and perfection will be attained within three years.
16.14cd: Contemplating his own body therein, he will obtain knowledge of the qualities.

16.15ab: By recollecting the blazing form of the *liṅga*, one attains the state of its Lord. 16.15cd: Meditating upon the *bimba* and so forth, as before, [upon] the tenfold [set] which consists of ten, 16.16ab:
one obtains the fruit residing within the covering of qualities (*guṇāvaraṇa*) without a doubt.
16.16cd: These twenty-four [dhāraṇās] have been declared, each being of five kinds;
16.17ab: These dhāraṇās of the elements beginning with earth are beneficial for yogins when practiced in brief.
16.17cd: Within the thirteenfold division, six others are established as follows.
16.18ab: These [states] are described for yogins so that yoga may be accomplished.
16.18cd: One should remember that after leaving the body, there is nothing else but one's own true nature.
16.19ab: Seated upon a white lotus throne above the three mandalas.
16.19cd: When one has thus become stabilized here, within just a month, the knower of yoga— 16.20ab: becomes completely freed from all diseases; what wonder is there in this?
16.20cd: Within six months, his higher knowledge (*vijñāna*) arises upon the surface of the earth.
16.21ab: After twelve years, one who is freed from old age and disease becomes a seer of the principle of the Puruṣa through three [years].
16.21cd: Right here, below the heart-lotus, one should visualize one's own body, twelve and a half finger-breadths in height, 16.22ab:
ending at the heart; by meditating thus for six months, one becomes a conqueror of death.
16.22cd: In three years, one attains equality with the Lord of the Puruṣa-tattva.
16.23ab: When the entire [process] is meditated upon there, as before, in the case of the Bimba and other [means], 16.23cd:
one obtains the fruit residing in the veil of the Puruṣa without doubt.
16.24ab: This knowledge of the Vedānta has been described in brief. 16.24cd: This was previously taught by me to Kapila in its full detail.
16.25ab: Contemplating his own body as resembling a mass of clouds at the autumnal twilight.
16.25cd: Within six months, he undoubtedly attains freedom from passion. 16.26ab: Freed from old age and death, he arises [perfected] in just one year.
16.26cd: After three years, he attains the great knowledge that removes the veil of passion.
16.27ab: One should contemplate the body as red, situated atop a full cloud;
16.27cd: for six months, without agitation, for the sake of attaining freedom from passion.
16.28ab: By recollecting this correctly for one year, one is not oppressed by death.
16.28cd: Having conquered the pairs of opposites in three years, one attains equanimity toward passion.
16.29ab: Meditating on the red [deity] seated upon a red lotus, extending five finger-joints down to the heart; 16.29cd: one obtains the entire previously mentioned fruit in due order.
16.30ab: For one who repeatedly contemplates the image and so forth mentioned previously, 16.30cd: there arises, without remainder, the fruit arising from the veil of passion.
16.31ab: One should meditate on a white lotus in the heart, having sixteen petals and possessing filaments.
16.31cd: [One should meditate on] the divine lotus consisting entirely of nectar, with its pericarp fashioned from the moon.
16.32ab: Having fixed one's mind there motionlessly at the end of sleep, 16.32cd: whatever one then sees in a dream becomes true for that person.
16.33ab: For one who practices in this way, the fruit arising from the lotus of the intellect— 16.33cd: all of that is produced for him through the application of its own temporal sequence.
16.34ab: Contemplating everything therein, such as a body four finger-breadths in size and so forth.
16.34cd: As before, one attains everything arising from the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*).
16.35ab: Starting from the heart, skipping over one and then another half-finger-breadth, 16.35cd: one should meditate separately on three wheels, red, blue, and black, respectively.

16.36ab: But the person (*puruṣa*) there, consisting of two or one joint (*parvan*), and possessing a splendor equal to that [of the previous], 16.36cd: and that which is called the *bimba* and so forth—this is the great triad of principles (*tattva*).
16.37ab: The wise know this division, consisting of thirteen [principles], to end with this.

16.37cd: Now, the two principles are described according to their elevenfold division. 16.38ab: One should meditate upon one's own essential nature, situated at the five-spoked wheel located at the limit of the pit of the throat (kaṇṭhakūpa), as if perceived by eyes that are ablaze.
16.39ab: Whatever entity exists on the path from the principle of earth up to the principle of time, 16.39cd:
having mastered it all, the lord of yogis is not overcome by time. 16.40ab:
Even when the reflection and so forth situated therein are contemplated by the yogins, [they are not overcome].
16.40cd: It is indeed a marvel that such a fruit is obtained without effort.
16.41ab: Day by day, the yogin who makes the mind steady in the space of the throat, 16.41cd:
obtains the fruit arising from *māyā*, even in the case of a reflected image and so forth located therein.
16.42ab: Resembling the appearance of a hollow in the throat, like the lunar orb swallowed by Rāhu;
16.42cd: contemplating this, he does not again fall under the sway of illusion and the like. 16.43ab: Contemplating that very [reality] there, as if released from Svarbhānu (Rāhu).
16.43cd: And one also attains a body of radiant energy and the state of supreme lordship.
16.44ab: One should contemplate [the deity] situated at the uvula (lambaka), having the form of the midday sun.
16.44cd: This is the collective form of the entire wheel of mantras.
16.45ab: Then, through the progression of time, the yogin attains the state of a Mantra.
16.45cd: And here, all the previously mentioned results are intended as incidental fruits.
16.46ab: Having meditated upon the Form (mūrti) right there, he shall attain the state of a Mantreśa.
16.46cd: Having meditated on that light as a lamp shining downwards, one should go to the state of its lord.
16.47ab: Recollecting it as pervading everything—both internal and external, as well as below and above—that person does not fall from the station of Mantreśvara, Īśāna, and [the other lords].
16.47cd: That person does not fall from the stations of Mantreśvara, Īśāna, and [the others].
16.48ab: Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), the yogi, recollecting the supreme seed-syllable, 16.48cd:
should place his mind between the eyebrows, slightly in front of that. 16.49ab: With eyes closed and a joyful soul, he should remain in a place devoid of sound and light.

16.49cd: There he beholds the Puruṣa, twelve finger-breadths in height. 16.50ab: One should fix the mind there; thereafter, after three months, [he sees him] complete in all limbs, consisting of radiant energy, and immovable.
16.51ab: With the divine eye, one sees a serene [light] resembling the moon;
16.51cd: upon seeing that divine person, the knowledge of the time of death proceeds. 16.52ab: If it appears headless, death will occur within six months.
16.52cd: There, the knower of yoga should diligently effect a deception of time.
16.53ab: One should meditate upon the stainless lunar orb above the *brahmarandhra*.
16.53cd: It flows with divine nectar in great abundance, filling one's own body.
16.54ab: Meditating for ten days upon himself as filled by that [breath] moving through the stalk of the heart, both internally and externally, one becomes a conqueror of death.
16.55ab: One should practice this yoga even for the destruction of a great disease.

16.55cd: For the destruction of diseases affecting individual limbs, one should meditate on [the deity] residing in each respective limb. 16.56ab: When one perceives [the deity] as smoke-colored, then a great disease shall arise.
16.56cd: If [the deity appears] black, one contracts leprosy; if blue, there is the danger of smallpox.

16.57ab: If the eyes are impaired, that disease [is indicated]; if the nose is impaired, that which pertains to it [is indicated]. 16.57cd: Whatever limb one does not see, one should diagnose the disease as being located there.
16.58ab: Whether of oneself or of others, the yogin established on the path of yoga [perceives this].
16.58cd: But in five years, O Īśvarī, one shall know everything up to the end of the reality of knowledge (vidyātattva).
16.59ab: One constantly knows and enjoys [it], and from that state one does not fall away.
16.59cd: When the light residing therein is meditated upon as pervading the entire body...
16.60ab: One attains everything previously mentioned through the application of the sequence of time for that [state].
16.60cd: Then, in that meditation which pervades the upward direction, one remains there unbroken.
16.61ab: Because of being the Lord of all the Lords of Mantras, one does not return again.
16.61cd: Thus, by recollecting [the syllable] with great brilliance even in the region of the forehead, 16.62ab:
one soon beholds it, appearing in succession endowed with eight colors; 16.62cd:
resembling sapphire and possessing a luster like that of a peacock’s neck.

16.63ab: Another resembles rājāvarta stone, and likewise another resembles lapis lazuli; 16.63cd: Another resembles topaz, and another has a luster like coral. 16.64ab: Another is like a ruby, and another has a luster like the moon.
16.64cd: Having seen that supreme moonlight, divine knowledge arises. 16.65ab: Thereupon, all activities such as wandering and walking on foot proceed.
16.65cd: When that which pervades above and below is meditated upon, one does not fall from that state.
16.66ab: Thus all this has been explained, established according to the distinctions of the objects of perception (lakṣya). 16.66cd: Now, the distinction of the mind (citta) is also taught in brief.
16.67ab: Through the pursuit of the eight qualities, beginning with the Piśācas and ending with Ananta.

16.67cd: One should make the mind perfectly steady upon the Lord, endowed with each respective form and quality. 16.68ab: Thus, for this path ending in the state of the Lord (Īśvara), [the methods] have been explained individually, according to the various modes of worship, for the sake of the yogis' attainment of yoga.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the Section on Concentration (*dhāraṇā*), in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*.
The seventeenth chapter, the Section on Six-Limbed Yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*):
17.1ab: Now, if all this that has been taught should not attain clarity, [then...]

17.1cd: When that which is unstable has been made manifest therein, the mind clearly does not remain. 17.2ab: Therefore, one should effect a cessation of its movement by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
17.2cd: And that is said to be fivefold, according to the divisions of inhalation (pūraka) and the others.
17.3ab: Inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), exhalation (*recaka*), and indeed withdrawal (*apakarṣaka*);

17.3cd: the fifth is to be known as elevation (*utkarṣa*); these should be practiced by yogins. 17.4ab: Inhalation is so called because of filling the air; it is described as being twofold and also sixfold.
17.4cd: One [channel] is filled by its own nature, while another is emptied and then refilled.
17.5ab: It is differentiated by the distinct openings of the nostrils, the mouth, and the upper palate.
17.5cd: Divided, it attains a sixfold state, and through further subdivisions, it reaches infinity.
17.6ab: The *kumbha* (retention) is to be known as fivefold; among these, one follows after the [inhalation] is full.
17.6cd: The second is proclaimed as that which is held after the exhalation (*recaka*).
17.7ab: At the end of the two [breaths], there are two others, and the fifth is that which abides in its own nature (*svabhāvastha*).
17.7cd: By means of its differentiation into other locations, this too attains infinity.
17.8ab: The exhaling breath (*recaka*) should be understood as being of two kinds, consisting of six [elements], as previously described.
17.8cd: The wind, having been stabilized in its location, is drawn upward from there.
17.9ab: That which leads to reaching another region is considered an *utkarṣaka* (elevating).

17.9cd: Furthermore, that from which one is led back to the original place is called an *āhṛta* (brought-back). 17.10ab: The *apakarṣaka* (degrading) is thus described; both of these are of many kinds.
17.10cd: One should practice these while seated in the *padmaka* or other postures.

17.11ab: The inferior [practice] consists of a single *udghāta*; the middling is considered to be double that. 17.11cd: The superior should consist of three *udghātas*, and it lasts for twelve *mātrās*.
17.12ab: Three times the duration of wrapping the knees [around the head] constitutes one *mātrā*; three times that, or three snaps of the fingers, is the measure.

17.12cd: One should not exceed the *ajitā* *mātrā* for the sake of warding off disorders of the vital air (*vāyu*). 17.13ab: By means of concentration on each limb, one should not fix the breath upon the eyes.

17.13cd: When the breath is held sequentially within the navel, the heart, the palate, and the tip of the nose, 17.14ab: four concentrations (dhāraṇās) are to be known, consisting of fire, water, Īśa, and the immortal.
17.14cd: Whatever substance one contemplates in each [location], one should remember that very thing as being omnipresent.

17.15ab: The form consisting of *bindu* and *nāda* is resorted to by the *dhāraṇā* of Īśānī. 17.15cd: One should meditate on the moon within the *amṛtā* [channel] according to the path described for the abandonment of time (*kālatyāga*).
17.16ab: By means of these *dhāraṇās*, the yogi established on the path of yoga [proceeds].
17.16cd: Having abandoned the object to be discarded, one should proceed to the state free from affliction.
17.17ab: These are considered to be the five types of eradication (samudghāta), numbered as three, two, and one.
17.17cd: By means of these as well, one attains the unsurpassed fruit described for the lower [stages].

17.18ab: Although the status of being a limb of yoga is equal [for all], reasoning (*tarka*) is the supreme limb of yoga. 17.18cd: Because it involves the discernment of what is to be abandoned and so forth, effort in that regard is praised.
17.19ab: Even when the mind has become steady on the path, [it may still waver] due to a desire for objects to be abandoned.
17.19cd: Having impelled [the mind] by that [means], one should lead it until the state free from affliction is reached.
17.20ab: The mind engaged in the cultivation of that object is declared to be *dhyāna* (meditative concentration).
17.20cd: That very [concentration], consisting of cultivation, is held to be the supreme knowledge.
17.21ab: Remaining there for even a moment, one attains meditative absorption (samādhi).
17.21cd: And when that [absorption] is fully perfected, one obtains the desired fruit.
17.22ab: Whatever object one contemplates, one does not perceive it as anything other [than its true nature].

17.22cd: Having attained identity with that, he subsequently becomes as if non-existent. 17.23ab: Having reached a state like that of the five elements, he cannot be moved even by intense [disturbances].
17.23cd: Then, through sounds and other [objects], the yogi, who delights the assembly of yoginīs, [remains unmoved].
17.24ab: Having repeatedly withdrawn the mind by this method, 17.24cd:

one should perform all the practices beginning with breath control (prāṇāyāma) for the sake of achieving success in yoga. 17.25ab: Or else, considering even every enjoyment to be deformed, [one should withdraw the mind].

17.25cd: Having abandoned his own body, he attains the eternal state. 17.26ab: Then, by means of the reverse procedure, he should perform the previously mentioned *nyāsa*, which possesses a radiance equal to the fire of time (*kālānala*), extending from the *skṛk* to the *chindi*. 17.26cd: [He should perform it] according to the inverted method, reaching from the *skṛk* to the *chindi*.

17.27ab: Having performed the fiery concentration (*dhāraṇā*) which inflames all the vital points (*marmans*), 17.27cd: one should fill the body with air from the big toes up to the vicinity of the head.
17.28ab: Then, drawing that [air] upward from the big toes, one should lead it to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

17.28cd: The knower of yoga should sever all the vital points (marmans) with this mantra. 17.29ab: Having placed the life-force (jīva) upon the first letter of the alphabet and joined it with the garland of heads and so forth, 17.29cd: he should then place a lifeless (ajīvaka) first letter before that.
17.30ab: Thus has been described this Night of Time (Kālarātri), which cuts through the vital points (marman). 17.30cd: O Goddess, he who desires long life should not utter this [mantra].
17.31ab: By the practice of reciting it fifty times, pain arises in the head.
17.31cd: Having thus reflected upon this condition, one should take recourse in the meditation that conquers death.

17.32ab: Then, having pressed it there, one who contemplates the *bindu*, *nāda*, and so forth, 17.32cd: should forcefully draw up what resides therein and release it into the Night of Time (*kālarātri*).
17.33ab: By this sequential application, O Great Goddess, even one who is merely a *samayin* is joined to the supreme state; 17.33cd: he attains the fruit described for initiation (*dīkṣā*).
17.34ab: [Lacuna] in the *Siddhayogeśvarīmata*.
17.34cd: From him comes success, characterized by all that is taught in the mantras.
17.35ab: That very [reality] is worshipped by humans in the form of mantra.
17.35cd: This true nature of what is to be known has been told to you, O Goddess honored by the gods.
17.36ab: You must never disclose this even to Guha, if he is not a devotee. 17.36cd: Having filled the entire abdomen, [the breath] reaches as far as the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
17.37ab: By means of the practice of whirling, one should then impel that wind in such a manner.

17.37cd: As far as the limits of the vital breaths (prāṇa) as desired by the yogins, 17.38ab: it is attained again by returning in that very same way to the region of the navel (nābhimaṇḍala). 17.38cd: One should practice in this manner for as long as seven days.

From that time forward, being joined [to the practice], he may draw forth even the gods (tridaśa). Having drawn forth by means of this the gnosis (vijñāna) cultivated by all yoginīs, one whose self is disciplined in yoga should grasp it; what is the use of other trivial teachings?
17.40cd: First, a great whirling arises for him through practice;
17.41ab: thereafter a trembling, O Goddess, and even more subtle than that, as if blazing.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, the Section on the Limbs of Yoga, in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*.

The Eighteenth Chapter: On Supreme Vidyā 18.1ab: Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret, unattainable by those of undisciplined self; 18.1cd: that which has not been told to anyone, I shall now declare to you.
18.2ab: Having abandoned everything else, one should fix the mind upon this.
18.2cd: One should not worship a *liṅga* made of clay, stone, minerals, gems, or other such materials.
18.3ab: One should worship the spiritual *liṅga*, wherein all that is moving and unmoving is dissolved.
18.3cd: Since the external sign possesses the status of a sign only because it is presided over by this [inner reality], 18.4ab:
therefore, one who has taken refuge in supreme non-duality should worship this;
18.4cd: O Goddess of Gods, by means of supreme meditation upon the subtlest atom.
18.5ab: Only he who has meditated upon it perceives this sign, and no other.
18.5cd: This which is called "vibration" (spandana) is firmly established within the heart. 18.6ab: By concentrating the mind there, both trembling and its arising occur.
18.6cd: Therein, the knower of yoga attains tranquility within a single month.

18.7ab: O Goddess, the *liṅga* has arisen from the heart and extends as far as the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). 18.7cd: It possesses stainless luster, illuminating the entirety of the body with its own radiance.
Right there, the one of great intelligence perceives the entire network of mantras;
having ascended to its summit with undistracted mind for just one month,
then, once that is fully perfected, all accomplishments [are attained] within six months.

18.9cd: He who, without understanding this sign (liṅga), relies upon the sign as the possessor of the sign (liṅgin), 18.10ab: His exertion is in vain; he does not enjoy the fruit of the sign. 18.10cd: This great Śaiva sign is not established within the sign of the Self.

18.11ab: When this is accomplished, the possessor of the mark (liṅgin), who resides within the mark (liṅga) yet is devoid of the mark, exists. What is the basis for this, apart from the mark and the marked?
18.12ab: When, by means of this mark and the marked, the yogi goes forth into the external world...
18.12cd: Then one should be known as a *liṅgin*; the *liṅga* is held to extend to the end of the city (*pura*).
18.13ab: From this knowledge of the *liṅga*, yogins are remembered as being "possessed of the *liṅga*" (*liṅgin*).
18.13cd: By means of this, the mantras are established, according to their divisions such as peaceful (*śānta*), fierce (*raudra*), and so forth.

18.14ab: What wonder is there that [these things] come to be for one whose mind has entered into that state? 18.14cd: If, having resorted to a fierce state (*raudrabhāva*), one should practice yoga, 18.15ab: he would become difficult to behold by all—gods, asuras, and humans alike.
18.15cd: Free from coming and going, with all views abandoned and without fear;
18.16ab: For as long as he remains for even a moment, for that long he shall attain this state.
18.16cd: Possessed [by it], he sees everything, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns.
18.17ab: That which is the imperishable, unmanifest, called Śaiva and also Bhairava;
18.17cd: having seen that, a yogi shall attain omniscience within half a year. 18.18ab: He who, having approached this very [state], attains satisfaction—
18.18cd: And he is not liberated from all bonds by means of artificial yogas.
18.19ab: Yogas characterized by breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the like are considered artificial.
18.19cd: Therefore, they do not equal even a sixteenth part of this uncreated [yoga].
18.20ab: By practicing this thoroughly, the yogi beholds divine signs.
18.20cd: Seated upright, the yogi should not think of anything at all.
18.21ab: In a mere moment, he may burn away everything within the body—both the unperformed and the performed.
18.21cd: For one who is being burned here, there occurs the experience of trembling.
18.22ab: Then, once that [trembling] has become steady, light shines forth within. 18.22cd: Having seen that supreme radiance, divine knowledge arises.
18.23ab: Even while enjoying sense objects, he attains the state of independent Śiva; 18.23cd:
as long as he remains for even a moment with his divine eyes unblinking, 18.24ab:
from that he realizes the all-pervading nature of the Self.
18.24cd: One should cultivate that very [state] with effort, desiring the fruit of all accomplishments.
18.25ab: Then the yogi, though trembling slightly, should cultivate that [state].
18.25cd: Thereupon, he beholds a radiance at the tip of his forehead on all sides.
18.26ab: Having beheld that supreme splendor, one attains divine knowledge. 18.26cd: Without effort, one succeeds within six months; within a year, one becomes fully perfected.
18.27ab: Having become equal in strength to Śiva, one goes wherever one desires.
18.27cd: Having made the mind all-pervading, the knower of yoga, in just a moment, 18.28ab: attains the state of being capable of entry, characterized by the experience of trembling.
18.28cd: Then, once that [state] has become stable there, after only a month, the knower of yoga—

18.29ab: He perceives the power of the Śakti as a steady radiance, both internal and external. 18.29cd: When that has been properly and perfectly accomplished, [he perceives] with care that which is born of all the senses.
18.30ab: Therein he clearly attains unimpeded higher knowledge (*vijñāna*).
18.30cd: And that which is connected with the meaning of the syllables [of the mantra] should be understood here as all-pervading.
18.31ab: Thus has this reality been explained according to its various distinctions.
18.31cd: Having set aside everything from the organs of action up to the intellect (buddhi).
18.32ab: The wise one should everywhere meditate upon the supreme power.
18.32cd: Having made the mind steady, until he has attained identity with it. 18.33ab: Until then, he attains the state of being omnipresent in a mere moment.
18.33cd: Having burnt away the nets of bonds, one shall obtain the fruit as desired. 18.34ab: Therefore, having made a firm resolve within oneself, one should practice this.
18.34cd: [It is that] wherein the individual soul (jīva), released from its substratum, attains dissolution.
18.35ab: That place is held to be the field of origin for all mantras. 18.35cd: It should be understood as being of two kinds, through the distinction between external and internal.
18.36ab: That [internal place] is known to extend for a distance of one *kalā* and a fraction (*adhika-mātra*), and it bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
18.36cd: Or else, as he is departing, the wise one should effect a cessation for a mere moment in the middle station. 18.37ab:
There he beholds the power of consciousness (cicchakti), lasting for but a single *tuṭi*, undivided.
18.38ab: That alone is the supreme reality; from it this world has been born.
18.38cd: In the Siddhayogīśvarīmata, that very [reality] is the mantra-body.
18.39ab: Embraced by that very [body], the mantras bestow the fruit of all accomplishments.

18.39cd: But that consciousness which one attains when the [mental] coloration has slightly subsided, being free from what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, is called the Śiva-principle (śivatattva). 18.40ab: By making the mind steady therein, one shall attain omniscience.

18.41ab: And there, one beholds divine signs without a doubt; 18.41cd: wherever in any part of the body a transformation arises, 18.42ab: preceded by volition, O Goddess, that is the reality, the supreme reality.
18.42cd: By practicing that with the desire to attain omniscience, the great yogin [proceeds].
18.43ab: Having enjoyed the perfections as desired, he attains the supreme state.
18.43cd: With devotion, the yogin should always [worship] himself with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.

18.46cd: Having concentrated the mind there upon an object being consumed by fire,

18.48cd: With the mind made steady at the upper aperture, shining like the rising sun; 18.49ab: Or likewise in the heart, or one may attain it at the "end of twelve" (dvādaśānta). 18.49cd: Then, within half a month, that very form is perceived.

18.51ab: From the bulb of the navel downwards, as far as the principle (tattva) above the crest-lock.
18.51cd: Resembling a minute star and made formidable by the flames of its rays;
18.52ab: at the conclusion of the power of the vital breath (prāṇa), one beholds the form of the Self. 18.52cd: Through practice, O Goddess, that very form attains full expansion.
18.53ab: That is recited as the mouth of all mantras in all tantras.
18.53cd: Therefore, within just one month, some degree of realization (saṃvitti) is expected for him.
18.54ab: By which he understands everything established within the heart.
